title: Shiprocket Eyes August IPO at Measured Valuation After Slashing Losses by 88%
content:
Shiprocket, the logistics aggregator serving roughly 400,000 Indian merchants, is expected to launch its initial public offering within the next one to two weeks at a valuation of approximately ₹7,000 crore (about $734 million) — a deliberate 30% markdown from the ₹10,000 crore (about $1.05 billion) implied by its most recent private funding round. The price is calibrated, not distressed: the company slashed its FY25 net loss by 88% and turned cash-EBITDA-positive for the first time in its history — a turnaround story unusual enough among India's logistics unicorns that it gives Shiprocket a specific argument for a lower but defensible public entry point.
Shiprocket IPO: What Is the Deal Structure?
The offering totals ₹2,342.35 crore (approximately $245.6 million) as a book-built issue on both the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) and National Stock Exchange (NSE). It comprises a fresh share issuance worth ₹1,100 crore (approximately $115.3 million) — the proceeds of which flow directly to Shiprocket — and an offer for sale (OFS) of ₹1,242.35 crore (approximately $130.2 million) through which co-founders and early investors will partially monetize their holdings. Notably, anchor investors Zomato parent Eternal, Temasek, and Info Edge are absent from the OFS sellers, a structural signal that the platform's largest institutional backers are not using the public window as an exit.
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) issued its formal observation letter on October 31, 2025, approving the offering. Shiprocket subsequently filed its updated DRHP in December 2025 incorporating its latest financial results. That approval is valid for 18 months from issuance, meaning the window runs through approximately April 2027. Axis Capital is book-running lead manager; KFin Technologies is registrar.
The price band, lot size, and subscription dates have not been announced as of this writing. Shiprocket declined to comment on the Inc42 reporting about its IPO timeline.
How Shiprocket's CORE Routing Engine Processes 620 Million Shipments
To understand what Shiprocket actually does — and why the IPO matters beyond its headline valuation — it helps to understand the technology that makes the platform's asset-light model viable at scale.
Shiprocket does not own delivery trucks, warehouses, or sorting facilities in the way that Delhivery does. Instead, it aggregates 17 courier partners — including Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, Shadowfax, and India Post — under a single merchant interface, then uses machine learning to route each shipment to the optimal carrier for that specific order. The proprietary layer that makes this work is called CORE, for Courier Optimization and Ranking Engine.
CORE analyzes more than 50 data points per shipment: the destination PIN code, the product's weight and dimensions, the payment method (cash-on-delivery orders carry substantially higher return risk than prepaid), historical carrier performance on comparable routes, current network load, and whether the buyer has a prior return history. A seller can configure CORE across four optimization targets — fastest delivery, lowest cost, highest carrier rating, or a custom rule set — and the engine runs those preferences against its routing model in real time.
Layered on top of CORE is a product Shiprocket calls RADAR, a real-time courier intelligence system that shifts from historical performance averages to live shipment signals. Where a standard routing tool asks "which carrier usually performs best to this PIN code?", RADAR asks "which carrier is performing best to this PIN code right now, given today's volume and hub conditions?" The distinction matters because logistics network conditions fluctuate daily: a carrier that reliably reaches a tier-II city ZIP code 95% of the time can drop sharply during peak season or after a regional disruption. RADAR's edge is statistical reliability — it requires the scale of 620 million-plus annual transactions to generate per-PIN-code signals that are not just recent but statistically meaningful.
The platform also runs a separate AI model for return-to-origin (RTO) risk prediction. RTO — when a delivery fails and the package travels back to the seller — is a structural problem in India's e-commerce ecosystem: cash-on-delivery orders, which are still common outside metro markets, carry RTO rates of 20–30%. Shiprocket claims its predictive model flags high-risk COD buyers with 82.5% accuracy before shipment, allowing sellers to pre-authorize confirmation calls or switch to prepaid-only options for flagged orders.
The economic logic of the aggregator model flows directly from this technology stack. Because Shiprocket pools shipment volume across roughly 400,000 merchants (of whom approximately 180,000 are active at any given time), it negotiates bulk carrier rates that no individual seller could secure independently. It then charges merchants a per-shipment fee and a monthly subscription, earning the spread between its contracted carrier cost and the merchant-facing rate. The AI layer's contribution is to reduce the most expensive outcomes — failed deliveries, RTO freight, customer-service contacts — which erode both margin and merchant retention.
Why the Financial Turnaround Matters for the IPO Window
The decision to target a ₹7,000 crore (about $734 million) valuation rather than attempting to maintain the prior round's peak is best understood as a calculated trade of headline multiple for IPO viability.
In FY25 (the year ended March 2025), Shiprocket posted operating revenue of ₹1,632 crore (approximately $171.1 million), up 24% from ₹1,316 crore (approximately $138 million) in FY24. Net losses narrowed dramatically — from ₹595 crore (approximately $62.4 million) in FY24 to ₹74 crore (approximately $7.8 million) in FY25, an 88% year-on-year loss reduction. Part of the improvement is accounting-driven: the company's ESOP expenses of ₹91 crore (approximately $9.5 million) do not represent cash outflows, and stripping them out reveals a cash EBITDA figure that turned positive at group level — ₹7 crore (approximately $733,000) for FY25, against a cash burn of ₹128 crore (approximately $13.4 million) the prior year. The core domestic platform alone generated cash EBITDA of ₹157 crore (approximately $16.5 million), more than doubling year-on-year.
The trajectory held into the first half of FY26: operating revenue rose 15.4% to ₹942.7 crore (approximately $98.8 million) and net losses narrowed a further 9.5% to ₹38.3 crore (approximately $4 million).
The ₹7,000 crore (about $734 million) implied valuation represents a revenue multiple of roughly 4.3x FY25 operating revenue. That is a more modest entry point than many predecessor listings attempted, and it may reflect the practical lesson from adjacent deals: Shadowfax, an Indian logistics company that listed in January 2026, debuted 9.19% below issue price and has traded in recovery mode since. Delhivery, the sector's most prominent listed peer, fell below its pre-IPO private valuation within months of listing. Pricing conservatively is not weakness in this market; it is strategy.
Where the Fresh Issue Proceeds Are Going
Of the ₹1,100 crore (approximately $115.3 million) in fresh issue proceeds, ₹505 crore (approximately $52.9 million) is allocated to investment across the core business and emerging verticals — of which ₹294 crore (approximately $30.8 million) is earmarked for marketing initiatives and ₹211 crore (approximately $22.1 million) for technology infrastructure. Another ₹210 crore (approximately $22 million) will be used to repay or prepay outstanding borrowings. The remainder is designated for general corporate purposes and potential acquisitions — no acquisition target has been identified or named in filings.
Shiprocket has a track record of acquisition-led growth, having previously brought in Pickrr (a competing logistics aggregator) and Wigzo (a marketing automation tool). The unidentified acquisition language in the prospectus suggests the company intends to continue building its ecosystem through M&A even after listing.
Where Does Shiprocket Fit in India's August IPO Wave?
Shiprocket's expected debut arrives in what analysts are calling India's busiest IPO month of 2026. More than 24 companies are targeting primary market issuances in August, targeting nearly ₹35,000 crore (approximately $3.67 billion) collectively. The pipeline includes Zepto (quick-commerce, targeting a fresh issue of up to ₹8,010 crore, approximately $839 million), OYO's parent entity PRISM (approximately ₹6,650 crore, approximately $697 million), Truhome Finance, and education platform Elevate Campuses.
The market catalyst for the wave is traceable to a single transaction: the ₹9,813 crore (approximately $1.03 billion) IPO of SBI Funds Management, which was subscribed approximately 42 times and encouraged companies that had been holding in the queue to accelerate their timelines. This follows a relatively soft first half of 2026, in which only 27 mainboard companies listed and average listing-day returns fell to 1.3%.
Is Shiprocket Still Losing Money — and Should Investors Care?
The answer to the first question is yes, technically, though the figure is shrinking rapidly. The answer to the second depends on what an investor weighs.
Shiprocket's ₹74 crore net loss in FY25 and ₹38.3 crore net loss in H1 FY26 are real accounting losses. But the economic picture is more nuanced: when employee stock option (ESOP) accounting charges are stripped out — an accounting convention that does not involve actual cash leaving the business — the group-level cash position turned positive in FY25 for the first time. The platform's core domestic shipping business has been cash-EBITDA-positive for multiple consecutive years by the company's own accounting.
The emerging business segment — cross-border logistics, Wigzo-powered marketing automation, and omnichannel solutions via the Omuni acquisition — expanded 41% to ₹326 crore (approximately $34.2 million) in FY25 but is still in investment phase. That segment's cash EBITDA improved 25% year-on-year. The IPO proceeds partially fund its continued build-out, which explains why the fresh issue quantum is meaningful even though the core business no longer needs emergency capital.
The structural question for investors is whether Shiprocket's aggregator-layer business — high volume, modest margins per shipment, recurring merchant subscription income — can sustain growth as India's e-commerce market deepens into non-metro markets. Sixty-six percent of Shiprocket's deliveries already go to tier-II and tier-III cities, the segment that most large logistics providers have historically underserved.
What Does the August IPO Mean for Merchants on the Platform?
One implication of the listing that the financial coverage often omits: the roughly 400,000 merchants who route their orders through Shiprocket have a real stake in whether the company's capital position strengthens or erodes. The aggregator model concentrates logistics dependency — a merchant who has integrated Shiprocket's APIs into their storefront, negotiated rates via the platform, and configured their post-purchase communications through Shiprocket Engage has meaningful switching costs if the platform ever weakens. A successful IPO that provides Shiprocket durable access to public capital is, for those merchants, a form of platform risk reduction.
The opposite scenario — a listing that disappoints and depresses the company's ability to invest in its technology stack or negotiate with carrier partners — carries real operational implications for a logistics infrastructure that now processes more than 620 million transactions per year across India's SME seller ecosystem.
Frequently Asked Questions
When is the Shiprocket IPO opening date?
Shiprocket has not announced a price band, lot size, or subscription opening date as of August 3, 2026. Reports from Inc42 and Economic Times suggest the offering could launch within one to two weeks of August 3. The company's SEBI approval (issued October 31, 2025) is valid for 18 months, so the window to list runs through approximately April 2027. Investors should monitor the BSE and NSE announcement platforms for the Red Herring Prospectus filing, which will confirm the timeline.
How does Shiprocket's AI routing work, and why does it matter?
Shiprocket routes each shipment through a machine learning system called CORE (Courier Optimization and Ranking Engine), which scores carrier options across 50-plus data points — PIN-code-level delivery history, product weight, payment method, and real-time network conditions via its RADAR layer. The practical effect is that a small seller with 50 daily orders gets access to routing logic built on 620 million annual transactions. The AI also predicts return-to-origin risk for COD orders with claimed 82.5% accuracy, which matters because COD failures cost Indian e-commerce sellers roughly 20 to 30% of potential revenue on affected orders.
Is Shiprocket profitable?
Shiprocket is not yet net-income-profitable — it reported a net loss of ₹74 crore (approximately $7.8 million) in FY25, narrowing to ₹38.3 crore (approximately $4 million) in H1 FY26. However, its core domestic shipping business has been cash-EBITDA-positive for multiple consecutive years, and the group as a whole turned cash-EBITDA-positive in FY25 for the first time, generating ₹7 crore (approximately $733,000) against a ₹128 crore (approximately $13.4 million) cash burn in FY24. The remaining accounting losses are driven largely by ESOP charges and the still-unprofitable emerging business segment (cross-border, marketing automation, omnichannel). The direction of travel — 88% loss reduction in one year — is the central financial argument for the IPO's timing.
What does the valuation discount signal about Indian tech IPOs more broadly?
Shiprocket's reported ₹7,000 crore (about $734 million) valuation is approximately 30% below the implied valuation from its December 2024 funding round. This is consistent with a broader pattern in India's 2026 IPO wave: companies are entering public markets at disciplined multiples rather than attempting to sustain peak-cycle private valuations. Shadowfax, the nearest logistics-sector comparable, listed in January 2026 at a 9.19% discount to issue price on the NSE, and Delhivery previously fell below its pre-IPO private valuation post-listing. The measuredness of Shiprocket's ask — roughly 4.3x FY25 revenue — may indicate that its management read those precedents carefully before selecting its price range.

title: Shiprocket Likely to Launch IPO Within Two Weeks at ₹7,000 Crore Valuation
content:
Gurugram: E-commerce enablement platform Shiprocket is reportedly preparing to launch its initial public offering within the next one to two weeks, targeting a valuation of approximately ₹7,000 crore.
The proposed valuation represents a decline of around 30% from the nearly ₹10,000 crore valuation secured by Shiprocket during its previous private funding round. The company’s investors include Bertelsmann, Temasek, Eternal, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, MUFG Bank and Koch Group.
Before opening the public issue, Shiprocket is expected to file a revised prospectus incorporating its latest financial information. The final size and structure of the IPO have not yet been confirmed and may change before the launch.
Shiprocket had earlier submitted an updated draft red herring prospectus for an IPO of up to ₹2,342.3 crore. The proposed issue comprised a fresh sale of shares worth ₹1,100 crore and an offer for sale of approximately ₹1,242.3 crore by founders and existing shareholders. However, the company may reduce the overall issue size.
The selling shareholders identified in the earlier filing included co-founders Saahil Goel, Gautam Kapoor and Vishesh Khurana, along with investors such as Lightrock, Arvind Limited, Tribe Capital, March Capital and Bertelsmann.
Under the previously proposed structure, Shiprocket planned to invest ₹505 crore from the fresh proceeds in its core and emerging platforms. This included ₹294 crore for marketing initiatives and ₹211 crore for strengthening its technology infrastructure. Another ₹210 crore was proposed for debt repayment, while the remaining amount was intended for potential acquisitions and general corporate purposes.
Shiprocket had filed its preliminary IPO papers through the confidential route in May 2025 and received regulatory clearance in November 2025. It subsequently filed its updated draft prospectus in December.
Founded in 2017, Shiprocket operates an API-led technology platform that enables micro, small and medium enterprises, direct-to-consumer brands and large retailers to manage logistics, fulfilment, checkout, payments, marketing and cross-border trade. The company works with logistics partners to help online merchants ship products across India and international markets.

title: Shiprocket Launches Fastrr, an AI-Powered Commerce Suite to Transform Online Shopping Experiences
content:
Shiprocket India's leading AI-driven commerce enabler unveiled Fastrr, an AI-powered checkout built to reduce friction and improve conversion rate at the seventh edition of SHIVIR, its flagship commerce summit. India's first AI-native pre-order suite, Fastrr brings together Shiprocket's evolving pre-order commerce stack into a single intelligent platform, helping brands acquire, understand, and convert customer intent through AI-powered experiences.
Held at The Westin Mumbai Powai Lake, SHIVIR 2026 brought together over 2,500 founders, brand operators, and technology leaders to explore how AI is reshaping the future of commerce. As Indian businesses increasingly adopt AI across customer acquisition, conversion, and retention, the summit moved the conversation beyond theory and into execution. Through keynote sessions, practitioner-led discussions, and live product demonstrations, attendees gained practical insights into how AI can solve real business challenges and unlock growth.
"We are at the point where AI is becoming table stakes for every Indian business. The founders who embed AI into the businesses they build over the next 12 months will create a compounding advantage that others will find increasingly difficult to close. Fastrr is our answer to that opportunity, bringing together intelligent capabilities that help businesses acquire, convert and engage customers more effectively through a single AI-native platform," said Saahil Goel, MD & CEO, Shiprocket.
As brands increasingly rely on multiple point solutions to manage the pre-order journey, their technology stacks have become fragmented and operationally complex, often resulting in disconnected customer experiences and operational inefficiencies. Fastrr addresses this challenge by bringing together Shiprocket's proven capabilities across the entire pre-order journey into a single intelligent, AI-native suite.
At the heart of Fastrr is Shiprocket's proprietary commerce graph, built from millions of buyer interactions across its shipping and checkout ecosystem. This intelligence layer enables Fastrr to continuously learn from every transaction, making its AI models smarter with every interaction. By bringing together frictionless checkout, AI-powered shopping assistance, anonymous visitor identification, Fastrr Ads, personalised WhatsApp automation and AI-powered conversion optimisation, Fastrr helps brands deliver more personalised experiences and convert customer intent more effectively.
A standout capability within the Fastrr suite is Fastrr Ads, an AI-native performance marketing solution powered by True Delivered ROAS. Unlike conventional advertising platforms that primarily optimise campaigns based on attributed conversions, Fastrr measures advertising performance against successfully delivered orders, giving brands a far more accurate measure of how every marketing rupee translates into realised business outcomes. By directly linking advertising performance with fulfilment outcomes, businesses can optimise campaigns with greater confidence, improve marketing efficiency and maximise profitable growth.
Fastrr reflects Shiprocket's belief that AI should not exist as a standalone tool, but as an intelligence layer woven into every commerce workflow. As the company's first AI-native pre-order suite, Fastrr marks an important step towards making intelligent commerce simpler, more connected and more accessible for businesses across India.
Shiprocket SHIVIR 2026 was co-presented by Airpay, with support from ecosystem partners including AWS, Google Cloud, Oneture, Salesforce, Zoho and others.

title: Shiprocket's AI push powers emerging businesses, as it awaits IPO window
content:
Shiprocket's AI push powers emerging businesses, as it awaits IPO window
ADVERTISEMENT
Shiprocket is sharpening its focus on artificial intelligence as it expands beyond its logistics roots into customer acquisition, checkout and merchant productivity, a strategy that founder and CEO Saahil Goel believes will become a much larger growth engine for the company even as it waits for market stability before proceeding with its proposed ₹2,500 crore initial public offering.
The company today unveiled Fastrr, an AI powered checkout platform designed to improve customer conversion rates, at the seventh edition of its flagship commerce summit SHIVIR in Mumbai. It also introduced Rocketizer, an AI assistant for small and medium businesses that connects business applications and acts as a virtual chief of staff.
Goel told Fortune India that Shiprocket's next phase of growth lies in solving merchants' pre-purchase challenges rather than just fulfilment.
"We are at the point where AI is becoming table stakes for every Indian business. The founders who embed AI into the businesses they build over the next 12 months will create a compounding advantage that others will find increasingly difficult to close. Fastrr is our answer to that opportunity," he said.
The AI push comes at a time when Shiprocket has filed draft papers for a ₹2,500 crore IPO. While declining to comment on timelines, Goel indicated that the company is prepared for a listing once market conditions improve, saying the company is waiting for greater market stability and investor appetite before moving ahead. He suggested that external market conditions, rather than business performance, are the key determinant for the listing process.
AI business expected to outpace logistics
Goel said Shiprocket's emerging businesses, particularly AI driven commerce solutions, are growing faster than its traditional shipping business and are expected to steadily increase their contribution to revenue and margins.
He explained that while logistics typically accounts for only 8% to 10% of an order's value, brands spend nearly one third of the average order value on customer acquisition and demand generation, presenting a much larger opportunity for Shiprocket.
"We were never a logistics company. We were just an integrations company. We make the ecosystem work together," Goel said, adding that Shiprocket's access to merchant and consumer data allows it to expand naturally into checkout, advertising and marketing technology.
The company is also investing heavily in merchant acquisition and AI powered pre-order commerce. Goel said Shiprocket already serves around two lakh shipping customers, giving it a ready base to cross sell newer products. AI, he added, enables the company to analyse millions of advertisements and leverage insights from consumer behaviour across its checkout network to improve campaign performance for merchants.
Held at The Westin Mumbai Powai Lake, SHIVIR 2026 brought together more than 2,500 founders, brand operators and technology leaders to discuss AI's growing role across customer acquisition, conversion and retention.
Meanwhile, the company reported operating revenue of ₹942.7 crore in the first half of FY26, up 15% year on year, while narrowing its net loss to ₹38.3 crore. For FY25, operating revenue stood at ₹1,674.8 crore and EBITDA improved to about negative ₹16.3 crore, supported by stronger adoption of its technology and merchant solutions. Shiprocket has raised over $426 million to date from investors including Temasek, Bertelsmann and Tribe Capital, and was last valued at $1.3 billion.

title: Startup Trends in India: Market Opportunities for Brands
content:
Startup trends in India in 2026 indicate strong ecommerce growth driven by beauty and personal care products, healthcare essentials, and high-value shoppers. Key insights include Peak order volume of 15.1 million in March 2026. Beauty and skincare leading consumer demand. High-value shoppers driving premium category growth. Organic and wellness-focused products gaining traction. Market corrections visible in May 2026. These trends highlight where startups should focus to drive sustainable growth.
What are Startup Trends in India & Why They Matter
Startup trends in India refer to the evolving patterns shaping the country’s business ecosystem, including ecommerce growth, customer behavior, product demand, digital adoption, and emerging business opportunities.
India continues to strengthen its position as one of the world’s largest startup ecosystems, driven by internet penetration, smartphone usage, digital payments, and rising consumer spending.
Understanding startup trends helps businesses identify fast-growing categories, optimize operations, and adapt to changing customer preferences in a highly competitive market.
Shiprocket Trends: Key Startup Growth Insights
According to Shiprocket Trends, startups in India experienced significant growth in order volumes during the first half of 2026.
March 2026 recorded the highest order count at approximately 15.1 million orders, likely fueled by seasonal demand spikes, promotional campaigns, and increased ecommerce activity.
However, May 2026 saw a sharp decline to approximately 917K orders, indicating possible shifts in consumer demand, category saturation, or reduced promotional activity.
The data highlights an important insight for Indian startups: while ecommerce demand continues to expand rapidly, maintaining long-term customer engagement and sustainable growth remains essential.
Order Volume Growth in 2026
Strong Ecommerce Expansion
The rapid growth in order volumes reflects India’s expanding ecommerce ecosystem and increasing startup participation across categories.
Digital-first consumers, rising D2C brands, and improved logistics infrastructure continue to accelerate startup growth nationwide.
Seasonal Demand Peaks
The March 2026 order spike suggests strong influence from:
- Seasonal shopping behavior
- Promotional campaigns
- Festive buying patterns
- Discount-led customer acquisition strategies
These demand surges create significant growth opportunities for startups prepared with scalable inventory and fulfillment systems.
Sudden Drop in May 2026
The decline in May 2026 highlights the risks associated with dependency on promotional sales cycles and limited category diversification.
Startups need stronger retention and repeat-purchase strategies to maintain consistent order growth throughout the year.
Beauty & Wellness Categories Dominate Demand
Skincare Leads Startup Growth
Beauty and personal care categories continue to dominate startup demand trends in India.
The most popular product categories include:
- Sunscreen
- Face Wash
- Face Serum
- Shampoo
- Natural skincare products
This growth reflects increasing consumer awareness around skincare, wellness, hygiene, and self-care routines.
Wellness-Driven Consumer Spending
Indian consumers are increasingly prioritizing health-focused and organic product choices, creating strong opportunities for wellness startups and D2C beauty brands.
The rising preference for natural skincare products also signals growing demand for sustainable and chemical-free alternatives.
Healthcare Products Continue Strong Momentum
Healthcare supplies and hygiene products remain among the top-performing startup categories in 2026.
Post-pandemic consumer behavior continues to influence purchasing decisions, with customers prioritizing:
- Preventive healthcare
- Hygiene essentials
- Wellness products
- Everyday healthcare solutions
This trend is expected to continue as health-conscious purchasing becomes more mainstream across Indian consumers.
High-Value Shoppers & Revenue Opportunities
High-value shoppers contributed approximately 5.1 million orders, making them a highly valuable segment for startups.
Although this segment represents a smaller portion of total customers, it contributes significantly to profitability and repeat business.
For startups, this creates opportunities to:
- Launch premium product offerings
- Build loyalty programs
- Offer personalized shopping experiences
- Increase repeat purchases
- Focus on retention-based marketing
Premiumization is becoming a major growth driver in India’s startup ecosystem.
Emerging Consumer Preferences in India
Shift Toward Organic & Natural Products
Consumers are increasingly preferring products that are:
- Organic
- Sustainable
- Wellness-focused
- Chemical-free
This is especially visible in skincare and beauty categories.
Growing Health Awareness
Health-conscious consumer behavior is driving strong demand for hygiene, healthcare, and wellness-focused products across India.
Preference for Premium Experiences
High-value shoppers are showing willingness to spend more on quality products and personalized brand experiences.
This trend creates opportunities for startups targeting niche and premium customer segments.
Key Risks for Indian Startups
Market Saturation in Skincare
The rapid growth of beauty and skincare startups may increase competition and customer acquisition costs.
Fluctuating Order Volumes
Sharp monthly demand fluctuations can affect inventory planning and revenue consistency.
Overdependence on Limited Categories
Heavy dependence on beauty and wellness products may create growth limitations if startups fail to diversify into new verticals.
Strategies to Scale Startup Growth in India
To achieve sustainable growth, Indian startups should:
- Expand into emerging wellness categories
- Focus on customer retention and repeat purchases
- Use data-driven demand forecasting
- Diversify product offerings
- Build premium product experiences
- Optimize inventory and fulfillment operations
- Personalize marketing campaigns for high-value shoppers
Long-term growth will depend on balancing customer acquisition with profitability and operational efficiency.
How Shiprocket Trends Helps Businesses
Shiprocket Trends enables businesses to track real-time ecommerce insights, category demand patterns, and emerging consumer behavior across India.
Brands can use these insights to:
- Identify fast-growing product categories
- Improve demand forecasting
- Optimize inventory planning
- Analyze customer purchasing behavior
- Build smarter marketing strategies
- Improve operational decision-making
Data-driven insights help startups stay competitive in India’s rapidly evolving ecommerce market.
Conclusion
Startup trends in India in 2026 reflect strong ecommerce growth, rising consumer demand for beauty and wellness products, and increasing participation from high-value shoppers.
While the startup ecosystem continues to expand rapidly, fluctuations in order volumes and growing competition highlight the importance of sustainable scaling strategies.
Businesses that leverage consumer insights, diversify categories, and focus on customer retention will be better positioned to succeed in India’s competitive startup landscape.

title: Building Bharat’s commerce backbone: The team behind Shiprocket’s rise
content:
Building Bharat’s commerce backbone: The team behind Shiprocket’s rise
From a broken logistics system to a full-stack commerce platform, how three founders and a leadership team are building the infrastructure that powers Bharat's ecommerce future.
Every morning after a dispatch, the same email would arrive: “Where is my order?” For small sellers trying to scale on India's early ecommerce platforms, it became a familiar and frustrating pattern. Not because the products weren't good. Not because the prices were wrong. But because once a package left the warehouse, it effectively vanished into a logistics black hole.
For Saahil Goel, Gautam Kapoor, and Akshay Ghulati, this wasn't just a gap. It was an opportunity.
What followed was not an overnight breakthrough but a steady build. Starting with a shipping aggregation solution, the trio began solving one layer of the problem at a time.
Over the years, that effort evolved into Shiprocket, a platform that is now powering everything—from checkout and fulfilment to cross-border commerce and post-purchase experiences for businesses across Bharat.
Goel, Kapoor, and Ghulati didn't just divide roles. They shaped the DNA of Shiprocket through the distinct lenses each of them brought in.
For Goel, MD and CEO, the starting point was always the seller. Having worked closely with small and mid-sized businesses in his earlier ventures, he had a front-row view of how fragmented logistics, opaque pricing, and poor post-order experiences were holding merchants back. That translated into a strong merchant-first philosophy at Shiprocket, one that prioritises simplicity, transparency, and control. Seamless courier
integrations, frictionless onboarding, self-serve tools: Goel's conviction was that sellers shouldn't need deep operational expertise to scale. Just the right infrastructure.
Gautam Kapoor, Chief Operating Officer, brought an operator's rigour to the table. His early stint at Jabong gave him a ground-level education in what breaks when ecommerce scales fast, and how even small inefficiencies in fulfilment or delivery cascade into customer dissatisfaction. At Shiprocket, Kapoor channelled those learnings into building a system where reliability is non-negotiable. Strengthening partner networks, ensuring consistency in service levels, holding quality as volumes grow: his focus has been making sure that trust, once built with sellers and consumers, doesn't fracture under pressure.
Akshay Ghulati's lens has always been global. Currently serving as CEO of International Shipping, Ghulati brings experience from Amazon, A.T. Kearney, and The Parthenon Group, a background that gave him an early read on how mature ecommerce ecosystems scale across borders.
Ghulati recognised that Indian sellers would eventually look beyond domestic markets, but the barriers to cross-border trade were steep. At Shiprocket, Ghulati built the bridge: simplifying international shipping, compliance, and logistics so that even small sellers in Bharat can access global customers without friction.
Together, they weren't just building a company. They were building infrastructure. And as Shiprocket expanded from shipping into a full-stack commerce platform, the problem grew in complexity. The next phase required leaders who could build depth across every layer: technology, product, operations, finance, and growth.
At the core of Shiprocket's platform is its technology engine, led by Sunil Kumar, Chief Technology Officer. With over two decades of experience across Oracle, Rediff.com, Reliance Entertainment, and EazyDiner, Kumar brings rare depth in building large-scale, high-availability systems.
At Shiprocket, he leads platform architecture, engineering, and data infrastructure, powering everything from real-time courier allocation to predictive logistics intelligence.
Translating that technology into intuitive products is Praful Poddar, Chief Product Officer. With prior leadership at OLX Group and Snapdeal, Poddar has spent years building marketplace and platform experiences for diverse user bases.
At Shiprocket, he leads product strategy across checkout, fulfilment intelligence, and seller tools, with a single-minded focus on collapsing complex workflows into seamless, self-serve experiences for Bharat’s merchant base.
Driving the core shipping engine is Atul Mehta, CEO of Domestic Shipping. With experience spanning Amazon and Unilever, Mehta brings a rare blend of operational rigour and consumer understanding. At Shiprocket, he leads the domestic shipping business, focusing on network expansion, service reliability, and partner ecosystem strength, balancing scale with experience in one of India's most complex logistics environments.
Shiprocket’s commerce growth layer is led by Gaurav Mangla, CEO of Checkout & Ads. A founder himself, Mangla joined Shiprocket following the acquisition of Pickrr, bringing a builder's instinct and deep understanding of digital commerce. At Shiprocket, he has built and scaled the checkout and ads ecosystem, helping merchants improve conversions, drive customer acquisition, and unlock new revenue streams. His 0-to-1 background makes him particularly effective at turning new business lines into meaningful growth engines.
Financial strategy is led by Tanmay Kumar, Chief Financial Officer. With over two decades across PepsiCo, Yum! Brands, Spencer's Retail, and Burger King India, Kumar has consistently driven growth and strengthened financial governance. He brings particular expertise in IPO readiness and public market transitions, a valuable asset as Shiprocket prepares for its next phase of scale.
Building the organisation behind this growth is Saumya Khati, Group Chief Human Resources Officer. With leadership experience across global consumer brands, Khati brings deep expertise in talent strategy, leadership development, and organisational transformation. At Shiprocket, she is focused on building a high-performance culture and strengthening leadership pipelines as the company scales as a technology-first organisation.
What ties this leadership team together is a shared conviction: that the future of commerce in India will not be built by a single marketplace, but by infrastructure that enables millions of businesses to participate and grow.
From three leaders identifying a broken system to a full-stack tech platform powering commerce at scale, Shiprocket's journey reflects a simple but powerful idea: build the rails, and the ecosystem will follow. And in doing so, they are quietly shaping what could become the most critical layer in India's digital economy, the commerce backbone of Bharat.

title: WNBA trade grades: Why the Toronto Tempo were smart to acquire Aneesah Morrow from the Connecticut Sun
content:
The Toronto Tempo and Connecticut Sun have officially inaugurated the 2026 WNBA trade deadline.
WNBA trade grades: Why the Toronto Tempo were smart to acquire Aneesah Morrow from the Connecticut Sun
The Tempo and Sun made a deal. With Aneesah Morrow moving from Connecticut to Toronto, which team aced the trade?
Aneesah Morrow is headed from the Sun to the Tempo in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and the rights to Maria “Masha” Kliundikova.
Let’s hand out grades for both teams. In the comments, let us know if you agree, and provide your own evaluation.
Toronto Tempo: A
Scuttlebutt swirled about Toronto’s search for a young big to pair with their backcourt of Marina Mabrey and Brittney Sykes, with reporting suggesting that the Tempo were willing to sacrifice their 2027 first-round pick in order to address this need.
These rumors emerged before Brittney Sykes was officially ruled out for the remainder of the 2026 season due to her foot injury. But even if Sykes was to return and play at the All-Star-level she had established and Toronto was to acquire a high-priced frontcourt upgrade, the Tempo were a long shot to make the playoffs, as they are now 5.5 games out of the No. 8 seed.
That meant they were risking sending out a lottery pick that could be the No. 1 pick in what is projected to be a loaded 2027 WNBA Draft. That would have been insane.
This trade, however, satisfies Toronto’s desire to add some oomph to their froncourt, without the unnecessary future risk.
It’s been an uneven season for Morrow (more on that below), but when given the opportunity, she’s produced.
In the 15 games in which she played more than 20 minutes, she racked up nine double-doubles. Overall, she’s averaging over 11 points and almost nine boards per game, albeit on shooting percentages that need to perk up. She’s a hard worker who’s eager to expand her game, even if her experimentation from behind the arc is still a bit ambitious.
Her relentless mentality likely appealed to Toronto, as it perfectly matches that of Mabrey and Sykes. And with two more seasons after this one on her rookie-scale contract, she is cost-controlled contributor for a team that, presumably, will be looking to add more talent in the offseason for a 2027 playoff push.
Morrow doesn’t solve all of Toronto’s issues. But, she certainly makes them better, both in the immediate and, more importantly, beyond. Considering Kliundikova’s inconsistent commitment to the WNBA, this deal was a no-brainer for Toronto.
Connecticut Sun: D
The Sun poorly managed Morrow’s second season, resulting in a poor return for a player with her potential.
As noted above, Morrow produced when given an opportunity to do so. On a team stacked with theoretical, young and developing talents that didn’t exactly fit together, Morrow and her archetype—an undersized forward who thrives on hustle—seemingly fell out, or in and out, of favor with Connecticut and their future vision.
Of course, with a new ownership and management group ready to assume control of the organization as soon as they decamp to Houston and become the Comets, it’s worth wondering if Comets’ voices, whispering into the ears of the Sun leadership, influenced the organization’s handling of Morrow.
After this Sun group drafted Morrow with a 2025 first-round pick, their decision to allot her an inconsistent role and then trade her for a future second-round pick and player who might not frequent the WNBA seems odd. This, however, is all speculation.
There’s more to Morrow. Yet, the Sun decided not to take advantage of all she has to offer, whether for their own benefit or to command more value in a transaction.

title: WNBA gameday discussion: Can the Dallas Wings prove they’re ready to achieve playoff dreams?
content:
In this season of overachievement for the Dallas Wings, there are still more boxes to check to confirm their status as legitimate championship contenders.
WNBA gameday discussion: Can the Dallas Wings prove they’re ready to achieve playoff dreams?
It’s the final matchup between the Wings and the Dream. Can Dallas finally beat Atlanta?
The Wings have wins over every team except three: the Minnesota Lynx, Golden State Valkyries and Atlanta Dream.
Wednesday night, the Wings get their third and final shot at the Dream (USA Network, 8 p.m. ET).
And no, scoring a victory over every team in the league is not a prerequisite to playoff success. However, a season-long ledger that feature at least one win over every opponent inspires confidence in a team’s ability to navigate the postseason gauntlet, proving that the team is prepared for any matchup, regardless of how the playoff bracket shakes out.
For instance, if the playoff field remained as is, the Dream, as the No. 6 seed would match up with the No. 3-seed Las Vegas Aces in the first round—and no one should be confident in Atlanta. Not only are the Aces the defending champs, but they have defeated the Dream six times in a row. Atlanta, rated as having the fifth-best title odds at 13 percent by ESPN Analytics, also has another resume blemish that raises skepticism about their championship ceiling, as they were swept by Golden State.
Neither the Valkyries nor the Wings are given current championship cred by ESPN Analytics, even as both teams sit ahead of the Dream in the standings.
Both teams, however, can continue to build resumes that, regardless of what the predictive metrics may spit out, put them in the center of any and all contender conversations.
After their winning streak was snapped by the Washington Mystics in the final game before the break, denying them from enjoying that elusive double-digit winning streak, Golden State returns to the court in the desert with opportunity to sweep the season series over the Phoenix Mercury (USA Network, 10 p.m. ET).
In the Valkyries’ home opener way back in mid-May, Janelle Salaün launched her Sixth Player of the Year campaign, leading Golden State to the 16-point win with 21 points behind a 4-for-5 effort from 3. In early June, the Valkyries held off the Mercury, powered by a near triple-double from Alyssa Thomas, thanks to matching 25-point nights from Veronica Burton and Gabby Williams.
It’s hard to see a thin Phoenix team reversing these results against a deep Golden State squad on Wednesday. The Valkyries should be right back to their winning ways.
Dallas, as alluded to above, faces a tougher challenge. Just as Golden State had Atlanta’s number this season, the Dream, at least so far, have owned the Wings.
More specifically, Rhyne Howard has owned Paige Bueckers.
Howard takes pride in her two-way player identity, and her league-leading 2.4 steals per game are proof that she puts in work on both ends of the floor. Howard, in particular, has risen to challenge when Bueckers has been on the other side.
The efficient brilliance of Bueckers, where she so often appears unbothered by any defense, has disappeared against the Dream. When the Wings lost to the Dream in late May, Paige struggled through her worst shooting night of the season, going just 3-for-13 from the field and scoring a season-low seven points. In the earlier matchup between the two teams in mid-May, Bueckers was also below her standard, scoring 15 points on 12 shot attempts.
The battle between Rhyne and Paige, of course, will influence the outcome of the game. But, there’s another factor that could, finally, help swing the result the Wings’ way: the Fudd factor.
The two games between Atlanta and Dallas came before Azzi Fudd’s breakout. She didn’t even play in the first contest, as she was sidelined with an injury. In the second game, she saw 21 minutes off the bench, scoring seven points on nine shots.
Since then, Azzi has more than acclimated to WNBA basketball, equipping Dallas with the kind of weapon who could solve their recent struggles against Atlanta. As a starter, she averages almost 34 minutes per game, providing a quieter version of the two-way play that defines Howard. Her two 3-pointers and more than 13 points per game also serve as a steady source of scoring production, achieved via ever-valuable floor spacing, for the Wings.
Plus, as proven by her four games with more than 20 points, as well as in her history-making 3-Point Contest win, she’s capable of catching fire—and then some.
In your opinion, would a Wings win over the Dream be meaningful? Is it important for Dallas, as they construct their contender credentials, to avoid a season sweep to Atlanta?
Or, rather than the big picture, should the Wings, as well as the Dream, simply prioritize starting their post-All-Star schedule off with a W? Does the desire make definitive statements about what could happen in the postseason distract from the day-to-day of the regular season, where only the next game matters?
Let’s hear your ideas in the comments.

title: Swish Funding Closes at $24M for Kitchen Growth
content:
Update — September 15, 2026: Swish has closed a $24 million funding round led by Bertelsmann India Investments, replacing the earlier report that the 10-minute food-delivery startup was only in talks for $20 million to $50 million. Existing investors Accel, Bain Capital Ventures and Hara Global also participated.
- The confirmed Swish funding amount is $24 million.
- Bertelsmann India Investments led the round; Accel, Bain Capital Ventures and Hara Global participated.
- Swish says it now handles more than one million orders a month across roughly 50 pincodes.
- The company plans to use the capital for kitchen density, supply-chain infrastructure and entry into additional cities.
- No company filing or announcement reviewed for this update confirms the previously reported $200 million valuation target.
Swish funding is now a completed capital event, not a negotiation. The practical consequence is that the Bengaluru company can add kitchens and delivery density, but the round does not by itself prove that 10-minute prepared-food delivery has sustainable unit economics.
Swish funding facts
What changed since the earlier Swish report
The earlier version of this article described a possible $20 million to $50 million raise and a valuation target between $150 million and $200 million. The new disclosure settles the financing amount at $24 million and identifies the investor group. It does not provide a verified final valuation, so the old target should not be presented as the outcome.
Moneycontrol reported the completed round and carried on-record comments from Swish co-founder and chief executive Aniket Shah about expanding within existing cities, entering new ones and supporting the kitchen and supply-chain network. Mint separately reported the same financing and interviewed Shah about the company’s multi-year kitchen plan. ETtech also independently reported the $24 million amount and the investor group.
Why kitchen density is the real use of capital
Swish operates a vertically integrated model: it controls food preparation, its technology layer and last-mile delivery rather than listing a broad marketplace of restaurants. That structure gives the company more influence over preparation time and menu consistency, but it also requires capital to open and operate kitchens before each local market reaches useful order density.
Shah told Moneycontrol that Swish now serves more than one million orders a month, up from about 630,000 when the outlet reported on the business in June. The company still covers only about 50 pincodes and roughly 40% of Bengaluru, according to the interview. Those numbers explain why management is prioritising deeper coverage as well as new-city launches.
A dense kitchen network can shorten rider distance, improve food temperature and spread fixed costs over more orders. The risk is that rapid expansion adds rent, staff and inventory faster than demand develops. The relevant measure is therefore not how many kitchens Swish can announce, but how consistently each kitchen reaches repeatable utilisation and contribution margins.
How the $24 million moves through the model
Everyone else is reporting the Swish funding headline; the more useful question is whether capital can turn a small geographic footprint into a dense operating system. More kitchens can improve speed and availability, but only if order frequency grows enough to cover labour, ingredients, rent and delivery costs.
The competitive pressure around Swish
Quick prepared-food delivery is attracting both specialist operators and large commerce platforms. The new financing arrives as rivals experiment with fast-food formats and use existing logistics networks to reduce launch costs. Swish’s answer is a tightly controlled kitchen model with a short delivery radius.
The contrast is visible in adjacent expansion stories. Amazon Now has crossed a reported $1 billion annualised gross-sales run rate, while Flipkart Minutes has expanded its rapid-delivery footprint. Those platforms can spread technology and delivery investment across broad product catalogues; Swish must make prepared food carry more of the economics.
That does not make the specialist model impossible. Owning the menu, production process and delivery promise can create consistency that restaurant marketplaces struggle to guarantee. It does mean Swish has less room for kitchens that remain underused, because food inventory and staffing cannot be deferred as easily as adding another digital listing.
What investors and operators should watch
The first signal is repeat demand. ETtech reported that repeat users account for 70% to 75% of revenue, a company metric that should be tested over time as Swish enters new neighbourhoods. High repeat usage can lower customer-acquisition pressure, but it does not reveal the profitability of an individual order.
The second signal is kitchen productivity: orders per kitchen, preparation time, waste and delivery radius. The third is expansion discipline. Management has discussed a long-term ambition to operate more than 1,000 kitchens, but the nearer-term evidence should be city-level density and service quality rather than the distant network count.
For India’s startup market, this follow-on round shows that investors remain willing to finance operationally intensive consumer models when usage is growing. The discipline comes after the cheque: Swish must prove that each additional kitchen strengthens the network instead of merely increasing fixed cost.
Frequently asked questions
How much did Swish raise?
Swish raised $24 million in a round led by Bertelsmann India Investments, with Accel, Bain Capital Ventures and Hara Global participating.
Is Swish valued at $200 million?
The earlier report described a valuation target of up to $200 million. The completed-round reports reviewed for this update do not provide a company-confirmed final valuation, so that target should not be treated as the closing valuation.
What will Swish use the money for?
The company says the money will support kitchen-network expansion, supply-chain infrastructure, deeper coverage in existing cities and entry into additional cities.
How large is Swish today?
Swish says it handles more than one million orders a month and serves roughly 50 pincodes across Bengaluru and Delhi NCR.

title: Quick food delivery startup Swish in funding talks with Bertelsmann India Investments months after previous raise
content:
Swish, the startup behind a 10-15 minute food delivery service in parts of Bengaluru and Gurugram, has returned to the fundraising market just two months after closing a $38 million round, underscoring investor appetite for the rapid delivery segment, people familiar with the matter told Moneycontrol.
"Swish has reached advanced discussions to raise about $20 million (Rs 190 crore) from Bertelsmann India Investments (BII) and other investors as part of a broader funding round that the company intends to expand over time," one of the people familiar with the matter said.
The platform offers a mix of snacks and full meals, with chai, poha and samosas among its best-selling items.
"It is still early days, but if the current discussions progress as expected, Swish could raise around $40-50 million. That said, the company may choose to close the round at a lower amount depending on how the process evolves," the second person said.
Bengaluru-based Swish is being valued at around $150-200 million pre- money during ongoing negotiations.
Swish and BII did not reply to Moneycontrol’s queries.
This will be BII's second quick commerce bet in under a year after backing quick services startup Snabbit in a $30 million round in October 2025.
Swish scale up
Since its inception in 2024, Swish's fundraising journey has seen several twists and turns. While the company attracted marquee investor Accel to lead its $2 million seed round in October 2024, its $14 million Series A round in March 2025 took longer to come together before UK-based Hara Global agreed to lead the financing, with Accel also participating.
A partner at a large global venture capital fund that evaluated Swish but ultimately passed on the opportunity said the firm's biggest concern was differentiation. "We failed to understand what Swish's moat is. Blinkit has Bistro, Swiggy is scaling Snacc, and Zepto is investing in Zepto Cafe – the competition is intense," the investor told Moneycontrol in mid-2025.
About a year later, Swish's fortunes had changed. In March 2026, the startup raised $38 million in a Series B round led by existing investor Hara Global, with Bain Capital coming on board as a new investor and Accel doubling down on its bet. The financing, which also included a venture debt component, doubled Swish's valuation to $140 million.
When Moneycontrol caught up with the same investor, cited above, about eight months later, the tone had shifted markedly. "We have tracked Swish ever since we passed – the turnaround has really impressed us. The team's execution has improved dramatically and the scale is looking impressive," the partner said. The investor still does not hold a stake in Swish, nor are they evaluating a purchase during the ongoing round.
A combination of stronger execution and a less frenetic competitive environment has helped Swish gain momentum, sources said. Since its Series A round in 2025, Swiggy has shuttered Snacc, Zepto has reworked its Cafe strategy and Blinkit has flagged sizeable losses at Bistro, reducing some of the intensity in the rapid food delivery market.
The gains are beginning to show in Swish's operating metrics. The startup is now clocking an annualised revenue run rate (ARR) of more than Rs 165 crore, with an average order value of Rs 220 and over 630,000 monthly orders, people familiar with the developments told Moneycontrol.
While Swish is still at an early stage, the numbers offer some perspective. India's largest food delivery platform, Zomato, is estimated by analysts to process around 2.5 million orders daily with an average order value of around Rs 500. The company, however, does not separately disclose these metrics as part of its quarterly earnings.

title: New Swish & Stitch scheme in Southport led by The Hearth will help families reduce clothing waste
content:
A new community project in Southport is set to help residents reduce clothing waste and build practical skills, thanks to funding from the Merseyside Recycling & Waste Authority (MRWA) / Veolia Zero Waste Community Fund 2026–27.
Swish & Stitch — Southport, led by The Hearth Network CIC, will deliver a programme of clothes swaps, sewing workshops and digital resources designed to encourage people to reuse, repair and rethink the clothes they already own.
The project was launched this week at the MRWA Zero Waste Community Fund event at the Gillmoss Recycling Discovery Centre, where community groups from across the Liverpool City Region came together to begin delivery.
Project Lead Rebecca Armstrong said:
“Swish & Stitch is about helping people feel more confident with the clothes they already own. A small repair or a simple swap can make a big difference — not just financially, but environmentally too.”
Over the coming months, the project will deliver:
- six themed clothes swap events at Southport Market, delivered in partnership with Enhance Events
- a six‑session stitch programme for young women aged 18–25 at Southport Community Centre
- a digital garment care hub offering simple repair and clothing care guidance
The swap events at Southport Market will provide an accessible and welcoming space for local residents to take part, while the workshop programme focuses on building confidence, skills and connection for a younger cohort.
The project also brings together different parts of the community, with experienced local volunteers supporting participants to learn practical sewing skills — creating a strong intergenerational element.
Swish & Stitch aims to reduce textile waste, increase reuse, and give residents the confidence to keep clothes in use for longer — helping to tackle one of the UK’s fastest‑growing waste streams.
More details on upcoming events and how to get involved will be announced in the coming weeks.

title: Unframe Acquires Swish AI To Strengthen Enterprise AI Platform
content:
Unframe announced that it is acquiring Swish AI, a company specializing in AI-powered IT service management and operations.
The acquisition will strengthen Unframe’s enterprise AI platform and expand its AI-native data capabilities. Swish AI brings expertise in helping enterprise IT teams automate workflows, improve service delivery, and turn operational data into actionable insights.
Founded in 2018 by Sebastien Adjiman and Arnon Yaffe, Swish AI has raised more than $20 million and is trusted by IT teams at leading global organizations. The company initially focused on IT service management, but its underlying technology was designed to ingest, restructure, and create a physical data layer purpose-built for AI.
Unframe said the acquisition will help broaden its ability to deliver AI solutions across enterprise workflows. Swish AI’s technology is expected to support deterministic, high-value answers for AI agents and applications running on top of Unframe’s platform.
The deal follows Unframe’s May announcement that it had surpassed $100 million in total contract value within 12 months and raised an additional $50 million in funding led by Highland Europe. The company has raised $100 million since inception.
By joining Unframe, Swish AI customers will gain access to a broader enterprise AI platform, additional technical resources, and expanded support for identifying and delivering AI use cases across organizations. Unframe said these use cases can extend beyond IT operations into workforce productivity, knowledge management, procurement automation, customer service, finance transformation, and other business functions.
KEY QUOTES:
“Generating real enterprise value from AI does not depend only on the model.”
“It also greatly depends on the quality of the data foundation and the ability to connect it to existing workflows. Swish AI has built an AI-native data warehouse that helps turn complex enterprise information into a usable base for intelligent solutions. Bringing Swish AI into Unframe will accelerate our ability to help customers apply AI deterministically across a broader range of enterprise processes.”
Shay Levi, Co-Founder and CEO of Unframe
“Swish AI was built around the challenge of helping enterprises work with the data created across their IT service and support systems and turn it into operational insights teams can actually use.”
“Joining Unframe will allow us to bring the capabilities developed in IT into a broader platform that can serve more teams, more workflows, and more business needs across the enterprise.”
Sebastien Adjiman, Co-Founder of Swish AI

title: Unframe Acquires Swish AI to Expand Enterprise AI and Data Platform Capabilities
content:
Unframe, a managed AI delivery platform serving global enterprises, has acquired Swish AI, a developer of AI-powered data and IT operations technology, in a move designed to strengthen Unframe’s enterprise AI platform and broaden its capabilities in AI-native data infrastructure.
The acquisition comes as Unframe continues a period of rapid growth. In May, the company announced it had surpassed $100 million in total contract value within 12 months and secured an additional $50 million funding round led by Highland Europe, bringing total funding raised since its founding to $100 million.
The addition of Swish AI is expected to enhance Unframe’s ability to help enterprises deploy AI applications across complex business environments by improving how organizational data is structured, managed and connected to operational workflows. As companies increasingly seek measurable returns from AI investments, access to reliable, well-organized data has become a critical component of successful enterprise deployments.
“Generating real enterprise value from AI does not depend only on the model,” said Shay Levi, co-founder and CEO of Unframe. “It also greatly depends on the quality of the data foundation and the ability to connect it to existing workflows. Swish AI has built an AI-native data warehouse that helps turn complex enterprise information into a usable base for intelligent solutions.”
Founded in 2018 by Sebastien Adjiman and Arnon Yaffe, Swish AI has developed expertise in applying artificial intelligence to IT service management and operations. Its platform enables organizations to automate workflows, improve service delivery and extract operational insights from large volumes of enterprise data. The company has raised more than $20 million since its founding and has built a customer base that includes enterprise IT organizations seeking to modernize service operations.
At the center of the acquisition is Swish AI’s AI-native data warehouse technology, which was initially developed to address challenges within IT service management environments. The platform ingests and restructures enterprise data, creating a purpose-built data layer designed to support deterministic AI applications and deliver more consistent, actionable outputs for both human users and AI agents.
Unframe plans to integrate those capabilities into its broader platform, enabling customers to deploy AI solutions across a wider range of enterprise functions. The company’s platform is designed to help organizations rapidly move from identifying business use cases to deploying production-ready AI applications that align with existing systems, governance requirements and operational processes.
For Swish AI customers, the acquisition provides access to a larger AI ecosystem and additional implementation expertise. Organizations currently using the platform for IT operations and service management will be able to extend AI initiatives into other areas of the business, including workforce productivity, knowledge management, procurement, customer service and finance operations.
“Swish AI was built around the challenge of helping enterprises work with the data created across their IT service and support systems and turn it into operational insights teams can actually use,” said Adjiman, co-founder of Swish AI. “Joining Unframe will allow us to bring the capabilities developed in IT into a broader platform that can serve more teams, more workflows, and more business needs across the enterprise.”
The transaction reflects continued consolidation across the enterprise AI market as companies seek to combine application-layer AI capabilities with stronger data infrastructure. Industry adoption has increasingly shifted from experimental AI deployments toward operational systems that require scalable data architectures, governance controls and integration with existing enterprise software environments.
Founded in 2024 by Shay Levi, Larissa Schneider and Adi Azarya, Unframe is headquartered in Cupertino, California, with additional offices in Tel Aviv and Berlin. The company enables enterprises to deploy AI solutions in their own cloud environments, on-premises infrastructure or through managed SaaS deployments, while maintaining flexibility across different large language model providers.
By combining Unframe’s AI delivery platform with Swish AI’s data architecture capabilities, the company is positioning itself to address a growing enterprise demand for AI systems that can operate reliably across complex business processes while delivering measurable operational outcomes.

title: Swish AI becomes part of Unframe: When an AI pioneer changes ownership – and still wins
content:
Swish AI becomes part of Unframe: When an AI pioneer changes ownership – and still wins

Language selection 📢
Published on: June 16, 2026 / Updated on: June 16, 2026 – Author: Konrad Wolfenstein
From niche player to AI operating system: The master move behind the Swish AI acquisition
100 million in 12 months: The incredible growth of Unframe – and the next big coup
The year 2026 marks a historic turning point in the commercial use of artificial intelligence: The experimental phase is over, and the era of consolidation and harsh realities has begun. While countless startups fail to integrate their promising technologies into complex corporate structures, the enterprise software company Unframe is breaking all industry records. With a contract volume of $100 million in less than twelve months and unprecedented customer loyalty, it dominates the market. But the true strategic coup has only just come: With the acquisition of the AI pioneer Swish AI, Unframe secures precisely the missing piece of the puzzle, considered the industry's ultimate bottleneck – a mature data infrastructure developed over eight years. The story of this acquisition is far more than an ordinary corporate transaction. It is a fascinating lesson in why technological excellence alone is no longer sufficient, how the enterprise market is undergoing fundamental change, and why Unframe 's newly created "AI operating system" could forever alter the rules of the game for enterprise software.
400 percent growth: The secret behind Unframe 's meteoric rise
The year 2026 could go down in corporate history as the year in which the gap between AI promises and AI reality finally becomes visible. On one side are companies like Unframe, which accumulated a total contract value of over $100 million within twelve months, making them one of the fastest-growing enterprise software companies in history. On the other side is Swish AI – an AI pioneer that had raised over $20 million, served clients such as Nestlé, Mondelēz, and Pacific Life, and has now found a new strategic home as part of Unframe . This constellation reveals more about the state of the AI market than any market research study.
Who is behind Unframe
Unframe was founded in January 2024 by Shay Levi (CEO), Larissa Schneider (COO), and Adi Azarya (VP R&D) – a team that previously worked together at Noname Security, a cybersecurity company acquired by Akamai for approximately $500 million in 2024. Shay Levi is an alumnus of the Israeli intelligence unit 8200, the birthplace of a disproportionate number of successful technology founders. Larissa Schneider holds a Master's degree in International Marketing Management from Hult International Business School in San Francisco and previously held senior positions at Nutanix and Noname Security.
The company emerged from its stealth phase in April 2025 with an initial funding of $50 million, now employs over 150 people, and has offices in Cupertino, Tel Aviv, and Berlin. The Berlin location is no coincidence: Europe – especially the German-speaking region – is considered a strategically important market for enterprise software, not least because of the high level of regulation and the resulting need for data protection-compliant, on-premises, or private cloud-enabled AI solutions.
Meteoric rise: 100 million in twelve months
In May 2026, Unframe announced that it had raised $50 million in a Series B funding round led by Highland Europe. Participating investors included Bessemer Venture Partners, Craft Ventures, TLV Partners, Third Point Ventures, Cerca Partners, and Vintage Investment Partners. This brings the total funding raised to $100 million.
The figures Unframe announced at the same time are exceptional: $100 million in Total Contract Value (TCV) in less than twelve months, with a Net Revenue Retention (NRR) of 400 percent. This latter metric is particularly noteworthy. An NRR of 400 percent means that existing customers have, on average, quadrupled their revenue with Unframe over time – an indicator of the so-called land-and-expand model, considered the gold standard in enterprise software. However, it should be noted that these figures were communicated by the company itself and have not been subject to independent verification. Such external validation is structurally rare in the category of early-stage, privately funded companies.
Calcalist identified Unframe as the second most promising startup of 2026, and the company made it onto Inc. magazine's list of the best places to work in the Artificial Intelligence & Data sector. While these accolades aren't financial metrics, they signal institutional credibility, which is relevant to enterprise sales cycles.
What Swish AI had actually built: Eight years of fundamental AI work
Swish AI – originally known as DeepCoding.ai – was founded in 2017 and has become a specialist in AI-powered IT Service Management (ITSM) solutions. The company has worked with prominent clients such as Nestlé, Mondelēz, Pacific Life, Coca-Cola, and CyberArk. In November 2021, Swish AI secured $13 million in a Series A funding round led by Dell Technologies Capital, with participation from Samsung Next and other investors. In total, over $20 million has been raised.
But Swish AI's crucial strategic achievement lies not in the names of its client list, but in the technical architecture the company has developed over eight years: an AI-native data warehouse. While ITSM represented the first commercial application of this technology, the underlying layer is universal: The system intelligently ingests and restructures data, creating a new physical data layer specifically built for AI—a so-called data enablement layer. This layer allows AI agents and systems to deliver deterministic, high-quality answers instead of hallucinating on fragmented or poorly structured enterprise data.
This technical achievement deserves more detailed economic consideration: By 2026, the biggest bottleneck in the adoption of enterprise AI will not be the model itself, but the data infrastructure. Research shows that over 50 percent of companies cite data quality and availability as the biggest hurdle to scaling AI projects. Swish has thoroughly investigated this very problem over eight years – a technical breakthrough that Unframe can now leverage as the foundation for its entire platform approach.
The logic of change: Why powerful technology needs a new framework
The case of Swish AI exemplifies a structural tension in the AI market. The company had valid technology, renowned customers, and institutional investors – yet still faced the challenge of scaling its business model commercially at the necessary speed. The acquisition by Unframe is the logical next step: The technology and the team are now receiving the strategic framework they need to reach their full growth potential.
What explains this paradox of technical strength and commercial failure? Several factors are at play. First, the company's focus on a single application area—ITSM—presented it with the classic dilemma of a vertical AI provider. ITSM budgets are managed by IT departments and are structurally limited in many organizations. The total market for IT service management was estimated at around $4.4 billion in 2026, a niche market compared to the broader enterprise AI market. Second, the transition from a specialized, single-area provider to an enterprise-wide platform provider requires not only technical adjustments but, above all, a sales and organizational restructuring that Swish AI, in its previous setup, was no longer able to undertake.
Thirdly – and this is structurally relevant for the entire market – the company fell victim to the capital market dynamics in the AI sector. In a market where investors increasingly focus on rapid growth and broad platform capability, specialized providers find themselves in a funding bind. Vertical AI specialists require longer sales cycles, more extensive consulting, and more complex integration work – all factors that consume capital more quickly than a horizontal platform approach.
