title: Ekal Houston Celebrates Ekal Yuva Udaan, Raising >$710,000
content:
HOUSTON: Ekal Houston’s annual fundraiser raised more than $710,000 to support education and empowerment initiatives for children in rural India, marking an evening of strong community engagement and youth leadership. Centered on this year’s theme, Ekal Yuva Udaan, the program underscored the growing role of young leaders in advancing the organization’s mission. From the stage to the front lines, youth played a prominent role in shaping the evening and Ekal’s future.
The program opened with the Ekal Youth Choir—comprised of first-generation Indo-American children—offering a resonant tribute to their dual heritage through the Indian and American national anthems, followed by dinner and cultural presentations.
The evening’s performances began with a traditional Panchari Melam performance by Houston Kalakshetra and continued with an address from Vibhav Aluru, a ninth-grade student who first became involved with Ekal at age 10 by funding a school with his savings.
Uma Dama, President of the Houston Chapter, highlighted Ekal’s commitment to advancing education, literacy, and empowerment in rural and tribal India, while also supporting local initiatives in Houston that benefit women and children. This mission was reflected in Studio Mudra’s presentation of Raghuveera, a superb dance performance featuring 42 Indo-American youth under 18, choreographed under the guidance of Guru Rashmi Sashi, which concluded to a standing ovation from the audience.
The event also marked notable growth, welcoming more than 100 new families and over 200 first-time attendees. Community participation played a key role in the evening’s fundraising success.
Youth voices formed a powerful thread throughout the evening, reflecting the impact of hands-on involvement and service. Vibhav Aluru shared, “It has truly shaped how I see service and impact,” highlighting how early engagement can inspire lifelong philanthropy. Kanishka Joshi, one of the youngest volunteers, noted that the experience helped her build confidence and communication skills while deepening her connection to her heritage. Anya Singh, a longtime youth volunteer assisting at the donation table, emphasized the level of responsibility entrusted to youth participants. Swara Bhatt, who has volunteered with Ekal for three years, added, “Having volunteered with Ekal for three years now, I love what this organization stands for. The values of education and compassion I have learned here will stay with me throughout my life.” Reflecting on the turnout, Rajat Nagu said, “It was absolutely amazing seeing so many people coming to the event in support of kids in rural India along with the fantastic organizers and volunteers helping everyone out!”
Ekal’s mission is to provide basic education to children in rural and tribal India through its one-teacher school model, with a broader vision of fostering self-reliant communities through education, health awareness, and skill development. With continued community support and an increasing emphasis on youth leadership, Ekal Houston is well positioned to expand its impact.

title: ShopKirana, Theobroma Scooped by Udaan & ChrysCapital
content:
India’s retail and consumer startup sector is seeing many mergers and acquisitions as big companies target specialized markets. This week, two major events highlight this trend: Udaan bought ShopKirana, and ChrysCapital now owns most of Theobroma. These moves show how leading companies are strengthening their main offerings by merging with or buying niche brands.
Udaan Acquires ShopKirana to Expand FMCG Dominance
Udaan, a top B2B e-commerce company, has bought ShopKirana, a startup that helps small grocery stores go digital, in an all-stock deal. This purchase will boost Udaan’s position in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) market, especially in smaller cities.
ShopKirana has a strong network of local retailers, good supply chain solutions, and important insights into the market for small stores. By merging with ShopKirana, Udaan can use these strengths along with its own logistics and technology to improve the ecosystem for India’s kirana market.
This deal also includes Info Edge, an early investor in ShopKirana, in Udaan’s group of investors, showing the strategic and financial importance of the acquisition.
ChrysCapital Buys 90% Stake in Theobroma
Meanwhile, private equity firm ChrysCapital has acquired a 90% stake in Mumbai-based bakery brand Theobroma, valuing the company at around ₹2,400 crore. Founded in 2004 by sisters Kainaz and Tina Messman, Theobroma has grown from a single outlet in Colaba to over 225 premium patisseries across India.
ChrysCapital’s purchase will help Theobroma grow. This could mean new products or entering new markets. The founders will keep 10% ownership and remain in their jobs. They will help maintain the brand’s core identity while also getting more money and support for growth.
The Bigger Picture: Why These Moves Matter
These deals signal a larger trend: big players are locking in market share through focused acquisitions. Udaan is securing its supply-side dominance, while ChrysCapital is entering India’s booming food and beverage D2C market with a beloved brand.
By acquiring deeply entrenched, niche players, both companies gain speed, loyalty, and market intelligence that would take years to build organically.

title: UpGrad completes Unacademy acquisition at $206m valuation
content:
Indian edtech company upGrad has completed its acquisition of Unacademy through an all-stock transaction valuing the startup at INR 1,955 crore (USD $206 million), around 94% below its 2021 peak.
UpGrad co-founder and chairperson Ronnie Screwvala disclosed the valuation to TechCrunch, saying Unacademy shareholders would receive shares in upGrad, while angel investors were cashed out when the transaction closed.
First announced in March, the deal expands upGrad beyond its traditional higher education and workforce-learning focus, adding Unacademy’s online test-preparation, creator and language-learning businesses.
The Competition Commission of India approved the acquisition in July, clearing a key regulatory hurdle before the transaction was completed.
Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal confirmed the completion in a September 1 post on X, acknowledging the scale of the decline from the company’s USD $3.44bn pandemic-era valuation.
“We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that,” Munjal wrote. “I’m not going to dress these facts up.”
The final valuation is also well below the roughly USD $500m valuation previously estimated for Unacademy when the companies announced the planned transaction earlier this year.
Yet Munjal maintained that Unacademy was not forced into the deal by an immediate need for capital. He said the company had around INR 900 crore in cash, annual revenue of approximately INR 400 crore, and that most of its businesses were profitable or close to profitability.
“Nobody was forcing this,” he wrote, arguing that joining upGrad offered a more compelling path for the wider education ecosystem than continuing independently.
This coming together is a strong message about collaboration. The bigger question is whether we are going to be a success factor for India’s workforce
Ronnie Screwvala, UpGrad
Founded in 2015, Unacademy became one of India’s most prominent pandemic-era edtech companies, raising around USD $880m across 13 funding rounds, according to Tracxn, as it competed with rivals including Byju’s for students and educators.
The company subsequently cut costs, laid off employees and consolidated company-operated learning centres with franchise partners as classrooms reopened, demand for online learning weakened and investment in the sector contracted.
The acquisition covers the entire Unacademy Group, including medical test-preparation platform PrepLadder, creator platform Graphy and language-learning app Airlearn.
The Unacademy brand will be retained, while Munjal will continue as CEO and lead its online businesses and Airlearn, according to media reports.
For upGrad, the transaction creates a broader portfolio spanning higher education, professional learning, workforce upskilling and online test preparation. It also gives the company access to Unacademy’s consumer-facing products, technology and extensive network of learners and educators.
Screwvala said Unacademy would bring stronger consumer expertise, product-led technology and access to a different target audience into the group.
“This coming together is a strong message about collaboration,” Screwvala wrote. “The bigger question is whether we are going to be a success factor for India’s workforce.”
He said the combined teams could bring radically different and innovative thinking to the business, while highlighting Airlearn’s international growth as an example of how Indian education products can gain traction globally.
Airlearn will remain within upGrad for now, with Munjal and Screwvala expected to decide in around six months whether to continue developing it internally or seek external investment, according to TechCrunch.
The relationship between the companies predates the current consolidation wave. Screwvala said Munjal first approached him in 2020 about bringing Unacademy and upGrad together, with discussions resuming in July 2025 as Unacademy considered its future.
The companies signed a term sheet for the 100% share swap in March after earlier negotiations had stalled over valuation differences.
The transaction follows upGrad’s acquisition of a 90% stake in internship marketplace Internshala earlier this year, also through a share-swap arrangement.
The acquisition offers another marker of India’s post-pandemic edtech reset. Byju’s, once valued at USD $22bn, entered insolvency proceedings in 2024, while other providers have cut costs, adopted hybrid delivery or narrowed their operations as investors increasingly prioritise sustainable growth.

title: Why Did Unacademy Sell To upGrad After Building One Of India’s Biggest Edtech Brands?
content:
Unacademy had around ₹900 crore in cash, a topline of about ₹400 crore and, according to co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal, most of its businesses were profitable or close to profitability.
Yet on September 1, it completed a sale to rival upGrad in a deal valued at ₹1,955 crore, or about $206 million.
So why sell when the company says it had the option to continue independently? Munjal’s own explanation points to a strategic choice rather than a need for immediate cash.
Unacademy Was Not Forced To Sell
Munjal has been explicit that Unacademy was not compelled to find a buyer.
In a post announcing the completion of the transaction, he said the company had “every option to keep going independently” and that “nobody was forcing this.” He pointed to its roughly ₹900 crore cash balance, around ₹400 crore topline and the fact that most of its businesses were profitable or near-profitable.
That makes the financial position an important part of understanding the transaction. The sale cannot simply be described as Unacademy needing capital to keep operating. The decision, based on Munjal’s public explanation, was about what the company could build next.
Munjal Chose A Different Path
Munjal said the deciding factor was the opportunity he saw in combining with Ronnie Screwvala’s upGrad.
He said he had met Screwvala several times over the years and was impressed by what he had built in higher education, as well as his vision for education in India and beyond. According to Munjal, the more the two sides worked on the combination, the clearer it became that it could be “a better path for the ecosystem.”
Munjal also offered a more personal explanation for choosing the deal. He said founders can sometimes be drawn towards a path that is more exciting than one that makes more money.
That is important context for the transaction. Munjal is not presenting the acquisition as an emergency exit. He is describing it as a choice between continuing independently and pursuing what he believes could be a larger opportunity with upGrad.
Why UpGrad Made Sense
The two companies also bring different parts of education into the same group.
Unacademy has a major presence in online learning and test preparation, while upGrad has built businesses around higher education, professional learning and skilling. The acquisition gives upGrad an entry into online test preparation, according to The Economic Times.
The transaction also brings Unacademy’s other businesses into the upGrad group. Unacademy shareholders are receiving upGrad shares under the 100% share-swap structure, rather than a straightforward cash payment for their holdings. Angel investors were cashed out at closing, according to Screwvala.
Munjal will continue as Unacademy’s CEO, meaning the acquired company is not simply disappearing into the upGrad brand immediately.
Unacademy & UpGrad Deal Took Months
The decision also came after an on-and-off negotiation.
Unacademy and upGrad began discussions in November 2025, but the talks were called off in January 2026 after the companies failed to agree on valuation. They revived negotiations in March and signed a term sheet for the 100% share-swap transaction. The Competition Commission of India cleared the merger on July 7, before the deal formally closed on September 1.
The final transaction value was fixed at ₹1,955 crore, according to The Economic Times. That was substantially below Unacademy’s $3.44 billion peak valuation in 2021.
Munjal himself acknowledged the contrast, saying Unacademy had “raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction” and that he was not going to dress up those facts.
Why Unacademy Sold
The evidence available from the company points to a straightforward answer.
Unacademy sold because Munjal and the company believed combining with upGrad offered a more compelling path than continuing independently.
That conclusion comes directly from Munjal’s explanation. He has said Unacademy had the cash and the option to remain independent, but believed the combination could be better for the ecosystem and its shareholders.
The valuation decline is an important part of Unacademy’s story, but it does not, by itself, explain why the company agreed to the deal.
The more immediate reason is the one Munjal has put on record, Unacademy chose the upGrad combination because it believed the combined path was more ambitious than going it alone.
Whether that decision ultimately creates more value for Unacademy’s shareholders will depend on how the combined business performs from here.

title: upGrad acquires Unacademy for $200 million; Gaurav Munjal says, 'The journey wasn’t easy. It never is'
content:
UpGrad, an Indian higher edtech and online learning platform, has completed its acquisition of Unacademy in an all-share deal worth just over $200 million, valuing the test-preparation platform at more than 90% below its 2021 peak.
Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal announced the completion of the transaction on Tuesday, acknowledging the sharp fall from the company’s $3.4 billion valuation during the pandemic-era boom in online education.
Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200M. We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I'm not going to dress these facts up. But I am proud of what this team did between those two numbers.…
— Gaurav Munjal (@gauravmunjal) September 1, 2026
“We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I’m not going to dress these facts up,” he said.
The transaction is structured as a 100% share swap, with Unacademy investors receiving shares in UpGrad. According to the Economic Times, the final value of the deal is about Rs 1,955 crore.
Munjal said Unacademy had a topline of around Rs 400 crore, with most of its businesses profitable or close to profitability, as well as about Rs 900 crore in the bank.
He rejected the suggestion that financial pressure had forced the sale, saying Unacademy could have continued independently.
“Nobody was forcing this,” he said, adding that discussions with UpGrad co-founder Ronnie Screwvala had convinced him that combining the two companies offered a better path for the wider education ecosystem.
Munjal will continue as Unacademy’s CEO following the transaction.
"The journey wasn’t easy. It never is," Munjal wrote in a post on Instagram.
"I remember once being up all night making videos just because our views were down and I didn’t want a month where we were not growing. Another time, Gaurav and I flew to China to meet an investor who didn’t even show up for the meeting. Whether it’s the sleepless nights, or the rejections, or the constant firefighting during good times and bad, it is a journey to remember. Very few people get the opportunity to create the kind of impact that we created. And I am proud of the impact we have created through Unacademy," he added.
The acquisition gives UpGrad a presence in the online test-preparation market, adding Unacademy’s operations across competitive examinations including UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE.
It also broadens UpGrad’s existing business in higher education, professional upskilling and overseas study programmes.
The CCI approved the transaction on 7 July, describing it as the acquisition of shares in Sorting Hat Technologies, Unacademy’s parent company, followed by its merger into UpGrad Education.
The companies began acquisition talks in November 2025 but ended negotiations in January after failing to agree on Unacademy’s valuation. Discussions resumed in March, when a term sheet was announced for a 100% share-swap transaction.
Unacademy reached a peak valuation of about $3.4 billion in 2021, when investment in Indian edtech companies surged as demand for online learning increased during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The sector has since gone through a broader correction as pandemic-era growth slowed, funding conditions tightened and companies placed greater emphasis on profitability and consolidation.
Reflecting on Unacademy’s wider reach, Munjal said videos by its educators had crossed 10 billion views on YouTube. He also pointed to four employee stock option buybacks carried out by the company, which he said had created value for employees.
Despite the sharp decline from Unacademy’s peak valuation, Munjal said he remained confident that shareholders could create significant value from the combined business.

title: upGrad Completes $200 Mn Acquisition of Unacademy in Major EdTech Shake-Up
content:
Ronnie Screwvala-led upGrad has completed its acquisition of Unacademy for just over $200 million, marking a dramatic reset for one of India’s most recognisable edtech startups.
Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal confirmed the completion of the deal on September 1, saying the company had officially been acquired by upGrad. His remarks also highlighted the extraordinary change in Unacademy’s fortunes: the startup once commanded a valuation of $3.44 billion, but has now been sold for only a fraction of that figure.
The transaction brings together two major Indian education companies at a time when the edtech industry is moving away from the aggressive expansion that defined the pandemic years.
Credits: Entrackr
From $3.44 Billion Unicorn to $200 Million Deal
Unacademy became a unicorn roughly six years ago and quickly expanded as demand for online education surged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The company attracted significant investor interest and reached a peak valuation of $3.44 billion. However, as students returned to physical classrooms and the edtech boom cooled, Unacademy began scaling back operations and focusing on profitability and sustainability.
The acquisition talks with upGrad reflected that changing environment.
Moneycontrol first reported in November 2025 that the companies were discussing a potential deal worth between $300 million and $400 million. Negotiations continued for several months, with valuation differences reportedly causing the talks to stall before discussions resumed.
By March, upGrad had signed a term sheet to acquire Unacademy through an all-stock transaction, with Munjal expected to remain as CEO.
The Competition Commission of India subsequently approved the proposed combination in July, removing a major regulatory hurdle.
Unacademy Says It Could Have Continued Alone
Despite the steep decline from its peak valuation, Munjal indicated that Unacademy was not being forced into a sale because of financial difficulties.
He said the company currently has a topline of around ₹400 crore, while most of its businesses are either profitable or close to profitability. Unacademy also has approximately ₹900 crore in the bank, according to Munjal.
That financial position, he suggested, meant the company had the option of continuing independently.
The decision to sell, therefore, was presented less as a rescue and more as a strategic choice.
Munjal said the company ultimately chose a path that he found more exciting, even if it might not necessarily have produced the most money.
That makes the acquisition particularly notable: Unacademy was not simply selling because it had run out of cash. Instead, its leadership appears to have decided that becoming part of a larger education platform offered better long-term opportunities.
What Does upGrad Get?
For upGrad, the acquisition fills an important gap in its education portfolio.
Unacademy brings with it a significant presence in online test preparation, covering major competitive examinations such as UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE.
upGrad already operates across higher education, professional upskilling, certifications and study-abroad services. Adding Unacademy gives it a direct entry into the online test-preparation market, where it previously had little or no presence.
The Competition Commission filing had specifically identified entry into online test preparation as one of the benefits of the combination.
The deal could therefore allow upGrad to build a much broader education ecosystem, covering students from competitive-exam preparation through higher education and professional careers.
Credits: The Economic Times
A New Chapter for India’s EdTech Industry
The acquisition also reflects how dramatically India’s edtech landscape has changed since the pandemic.
Companies that once raised money at billion-dollar valuations are now being forced to prioritise sustainable growth, profitability and efficient operations rather than expansion at any cost.
The transaction follows a ₹360 crore internal funding round at upGrad, in which Screwvala invested ₹300 crore, with Temasek, IFC and 360 One also participating.
For Unacademy, the deal closes one chapter of its remarkable startup journey. For upGrad, it opens another—with access to a large test-preparation business and an established brand that became synonymous with India’s online education boom.
The bigger question now is whether the combination can turn two very different journeys into a stronger, more sustainable education business.

title: upGrad Completes Unacademy Acquisition at Just Over $200 Million
content:
upGrad has completed its acquisition of Unacademy in an all-stock transaction valued at just over $200 million, closing one of the most significant consolidation deals in India’s education-technology sector. Unacademy co-founder and chief executive Gaurav Munjal confirmed the completion on September 1 following months of negotiations and regulatory review.
The combination gives upGrad a substantial position in online competitive-examination preparation, complementing its existing businesses in higher education, professional upskilling, enterprise learning and study-abroad services. Unacademy’s core portfolio spans preparation for examinations including UPSC, NEET PG and CAT, along with online learning products built around educators, recorded courses and live instruction.
The transaction was structured as a 100% share swap. When the term sheet was signed in March, upGrad co-founder Ronnie Screwvala said Munjal would remain responsible for Unacademy and continue developing its online education products. The Competition Commission of India approved the proposed combination in July, clearing the principal competition-law requirement before closure. The confirmed closing ends negotiations that had previously stalled over valuation.
The final price represents a substantial reset from Unacademy’s $3.44 billion peak valuation during the pandemic-era expansion of online education. The company has raised more than $830 million from investors including SoftBank, Peak XV Partners, Elevation Capital, Blume Ventures and Meta. Munjal acknowledged the difference between the amount raised at the market peak and the eventual sale value while stating that the company was not compelled to transact because of an immediate cash shortage.
At closing, Unacademy had annual topline of approximately Rs 400 crore and about Rs 900 crore in cash, based on figures disclosed by Munjal. He said most of its businesses were profitable or approaching profitability. The company had spent several years reducing costs, narrowing its operating footprint and concentrating resources on its core test-preparation operations after the wider edtech market corrected from pandemic-era growth assumptions.
During the earlier restructuring, Unacademy reduced the annual cash burn in its test-preparation business from roughly Rs 450 crore to about Rs 200 crore. Several examination categories, including UPSC, NEET PG and CAT, had reached positive contribution margins. The acquisition therefore combines a leaner test-preparation business with upGrad’s larger portfolio of career-linked education services.
For upGrad, the deal adds a consumer learning brand and a large competitive-exam category to a group historically centred on working professionals, university-linked programmes and corporate training. For Unacademy, the share-swap structure preserves participation in the combined business while placing its operations inside a broader education platform. Transaction disclosures put the final valuation more than 94% below Unacademy’s 2021 peak, making the closing a prominent marker of the sector’s post-boom consolidation.

Unacademy was among the most prominent beneficiaries of the surge in online learning during the pandemic.

Since then, management has shifted its focus towards sustainability and profitability.

- Most business units either profitable or near-profitable

The acquisition comes amid a broader restructuring of India's edtech market.
After years of rapid expansion fuelled by abundant venture capital, many companies have shifted their focus towards profitability, operational efficiency and sustainable growth.

What comes next
With regulatory approvals secured and the acquisition formally completed, attention will now turn to integration and growth.

For Unacademy, it marks the beginning of a new chapter after a journey that saw the company rise to unicorn status before navigating a dramatically different funding and operating environment.
The deal stands as one of the most significant edtech transactions in recent years and could signal further consolidation across the sector as companies adapt to a more disciplined growth era.

As the acquisition was completed, Unacademy co-founder Roman Saini looked back on the journey that began during his time at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), when he decided to quit the civil services and build the company with Munjal.
“It has been one helluva journey since that stroll in LBSNAA when I was on the phone with @gauravmunjal and decided to quit IAS and build Unacademy," Saini said in a post.
He recalled how Unacademy grew dramatically during the Covid-19 pandemic, when more than 100,000 live classes were being conducted on the platform every month and the company had nearly one million paid subscribers.
Saini also remembered meeting a CISF officer during a flight who recognised him and thanked him for making online education available to people who could not attend offline coaching centres while continuing to work.
“When we started posting videos on YouTube, very few smart people were teaching online," Saini said, recalling a time when becoming an online educator was still looked down upon.
He said he personally called around 200 people during the first month to persuade them to teach online. The platform subsequently grew from millions of views to billions, while many of India’s leading educators eventually taught on Unacademy.
‘The Journey Wasn’t Easy’
Saini also recalled some of the more difficult periods in Unacademy’s growth, including staying up through the night to make videos when views declined because he did not want the company to record a month without growth.
He also remembered travelling with Munjal to China for a meeting with an investor who did not turn up.
“Whether it’s the sleepless nights, or the rejections, or the constant firefighting during good times and bad, it is a journey to remember," Saini said.
He said he was proud of the impact Unacademy had created in India’s education ecosystem and described the opportunity to build the company as one that “very few people get".
“And now, as a part of upGrad, we are looking forward to creating an even bigger dent in the universe with @RonnieScrewvala," Saini said.
What Happens To Unacademy Now?
Unacademy, PrepLadder, AirLearn and Graphy will operate from Bengaluru following the transaction, with PrepLadder’s headquarters shifting from Chandigarh.
Unacademy’s educators have collectively crossed 10 billion views on YouTube, while its language-learning platform AirLearn has become one of the world’s three most-downloaded language-learning apps in less than two years.
AirLearn will also become part of UpGrad following the transaction.
The companies began negotiations in November 2025 but called off talks in January after failing to agree on valuation. Discussions resumed in March, when Munjal and Screwvala announced a term sheet for a 100% share swap carrying a break fee.
The Competition Commission of India cleared the merger on July 7.
Unacademy has also completed an employee stock option exercise worth ₹45 crore, with around 1,000 of its 1,100 former employees participating.
The acquisition gives UpGrad an entry into the online test-preparation segment and is expected to strengthen its position across India’s education and upskilling market.
Quick Answers
This acquisition signals a broader shift in the Indian edtech market toward consolidation, profitability, and AI-led, enterprise-focused growth. It highlights a trend where surviving independently has become difficult for single-segment edtech businesses, making equity-sharing and mergers more common than expensive cash exits. Additionally, the deal creates a larger integrated platform spanning test preparation, higher education, and professional upskilling.

title: Unacademy completes deal with Screwvala's upGrad at $200 mn valuation
content:
Unacademy completes deal with Screwvala's upGrad at $200 mn valuation
Unacademy CEO Gaurav Munjal said the company chose the upGrad deal despite having Rs 900 crore in cash and the option to continue independently, calling it "the more ambitious path"
Listen to This Article
Unacademy Group has completed its acquisition by Ronnie Screwvala-led upskilling firm upGrad in an all-stock transaction that values the education company at just over $200 million. This marks a 94 per cent decline for Unacademy from its peak valuation of around $3.4 billion in 2021.
 
The deal, first outlined in a term sheet signed in March 2026 and approved by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) in July, closed on Tuesday. SoftBank-backed Unacademy shareholders will receive shares in upGrad as consideration for the transaction.
 
The transaction covers the entire Unacademy Group and all of its operating entities. It brings together upGrad’s higher education, study-abroad, careers and enterprise upskilling businesses with Unacademy’s portfolio spanning competitive exam preparation, creator monetisation and language learning.
 
Gaurav Munjal continues as CEO of Unacademy and will lead the Unacademy Group of businesses within upGrad. At the time of closing, the Unacademy Group said it had a topline of approximately Rs 400 crore, with most business lines profitable or approaching profitability, and approximately Rs 900 crore in cash on its balance sheet.
 
“We built products that became the template for the Indian education sector. We had Rs 900 crore in the bank and every option to keep going alone. We chose this instead, because building it with Ronnie, together with upGrad, is the more ambitious path, not the safer one,” said Gaurav Munjal, co-founder and CEO, Unacademy Group.
Also Read
Across its platforms, the group said it has built one of the largest learning audiences in India and, more recently, outside it. Videos from educators on Unacademy’s free platform have crossed 10 billion views on YouTube. It said Airlearn, launched two years ago, has become one of the three most downloaded language-learning apps in the world, with 10 million learners across more than 150 countries.
 
“With upGrad and Unacademy coming together, we will now reach learners at every stage, from their first competitive exam to the last skill they pick up at work. This isn't just a bigger company; it's a bigger responsibility, and a much bigger chance to change outcomes. That's what I'm really excited about,” said Ronnie Screwvala, co-founder and chairperson, upGrad.
All Unacademy Group products continue to operate without disruption. Existing subscriptions, courses, batches and educator agreements remain in force, and learners will see no change to their access.
 
Unacademy Group teams move across to upGrad with the businesses they run. Over the past three years, the company completed four ESOP buybacks, returning value to employees.
 
Together, the two companies will operate across the full span of learning, from competitive exams to higher education, professional upskilling and careers, while continuing to build consumer products for learners globally.
 
Earlier, upGrad had walked away from talks to acquire Unacademy, ending one of the edtech sector’s most closely watched deal discussions amid differences over valuation. The collapse followed an earlier failed sale effort by Unacademy. In 2024, the company held talks with Kota-based Allen Career Institute, which also fell apart over valuation disagreements. These developments came amid a turbulent period that included pushback over changes to its ESOP policy. The edtech firm also had plans to transition fully to a franchise-led offline model, sources said, amid a tougher funding and consolidation environment for the sector.

title: upGrad Completes $200 Million Acquisition of Unacademy in All-Stock Deal
content:
upGrad Completes $200 Million Acquisition of Unacademy in All-Stock Deal
India's edtech sector just witnessed one of its most symbolic consolidations. upGrad, the higher-education and professional-learning platform led by media veteran Ronnie Screwvala, has finalized its acquisition of test-preparation pioneer Unacademy for just over $200 million.
The all-stock transaction, announced Tuesday, brings Unacademy's portfolio—spanning competitive exams like UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE—under upGrad's umbrella. It also includes Airlearn, Unacademy's language-learning app that has rapidly climbed global download charts. Unacademy investors will receive one seat on upGrad's board as part of the arrangement, which was valued at approximately ₹1,955 crore.
For Gaurav Munjal, Unacademy's co-founder and CEO, the closing marks the end of a journey that began exactly six years ago when the company achieved unicorn status. In a post on X, he acknowledged the stark contrast between past ambition and present reality. "Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200M," he wrote, adding, "We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that."
Unacademy reached a peak valuation of $3.44 billion in 2021, making the acquisition price a decline of more than 90%. Yet Munjal framed the decision as strategic rather than forced. The company, he said, had a topline of around ₹400 crore and ₹900 crore in cash—enough runway to continue independently. "Nobody was forcing this. But sometimes, you are drawn towards a path that is more exciting than the one that makes you more money," he wrote.
A Deal Years in the Making
The path to closing was neither short nor smooth. Discussions between the two companies first surfaced in November 2024, only to be called off in January amid disagreements over valuation. The talks revived in March with the share-swap structure that ultimately carried the deal forward. The Competition Commission of India cleared the combination on July 7.
Screwvala, announcing the acquisition on LinkedIn, traced the relationship back even further. The first conversation, he said, occurred in 2020 when Munjal approached him and upGrad co-founder Mayank Kumar about merging the two companies. Munjal reportedly proposed running the combined entity at the time, an idea that was not pursued. But Screwvala said the approach demonstrated "the quality and level of what Unacademy was building," and the relationship continued over the years.
When Munjal reached out again in July 2025, the circumstances were different. Screwvala credited Munjal's transparency about Unacademy's situation with creating the conditions for the deal to proceed. "The more we did, the clearer it got: this is a better path for the ecosystem, not just for us," Munjal wrote in his post.
Complementary Strengths
The acquisition unites two edtech models that evolved along divergent paths. upGrad built its reputation in higher education, professional certifications, study-abroad services and workforce upskilling. Unacademy, by contrast, became synonymous with consumer-facing test preparation, leveraging a free YouTube-based model that turned educators into widely recognized figures.
Munjal highlighted that Unacademy's educators have generated more than 100 billion views on YouTube, a figure he said reflected the platform's role in creating "a generation of celebrity educators." Airlearn, meanwhile, became one of the world's three most-downloaded language-learning apps within two years of launch—a point of particular pride for Munjal, who noted, "We always wanted to build a global consumer product out of India. We did."
Screwvala pointed to Unacademy's product and technology-led thinking, brand strength, access to a different target audience, and team resilience as key assets. He described the completion as a coming together of the two teams and said he expected "incredible synergies" as the businesses integrate.
Sector Consolidation Accelerates
The transaction reflects a broader shift in India's edtech landscape. During the pandemic, the sector experienced explosive growth and soaring valuations as students moved online en masse. That period has given way to a more sober era focused on profitability, operational sustainability and consolidation.
Note: Figures reflect statements by company leadership at the time of the acquisition announcement.
Munjal will continue to lead Unacademy under the new ownership structure. In his post, he thanked a roster of fellow founders and investors—including Shailendra Singh, Deepinder Goyal, Bhavin Turakhia, Sujeet Kumar, Bhavish Aggarwal, Aakrit Vaish, Mukul Arora, Shantanu Rastogi and Karthik Reddy—saying he might have "personally given up when things got really hard" without their support.
The deal, he suggested, was less about financial necessity than about pursuing a more compelling path forward. "I always walked away with the thought that it would be fantastic to work with him," Munjal wrote of Screwvala, whose vision for education in India he said had long inspired him.

title: ‘We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction’: Gaurav Munjal on Unacademy-upGrad deal
content:
New Delhi: Unacademy has completed its acquisition by upGrad for just over $200 million, six years after the edtech company became a unicorn, according to Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal.
Announcing the completion of the transaction on X, Munjal acknowledged the gap between the company’s earlier fundraising phase and the eventual acquisition value.
Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200M. We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I'm not going to dress these facts up. But I am proud of what this team did between those two numbers.…
— Gaurav Munjal (@gauravmunjal) September 1, 2026
“Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200M. We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I'm not going to dress these facts up,” Munjal wrote.
He said he remained proud of what the company had built during that period, pointing to Unacademy’s educator ecosystem and its expansion into products such as language-learning platform Airlearn.
Munjal also said the transaction was not prompted by an immediate need for capital. According to him, Unacademy currently has a topline of around Rs 400 crore, most of its businesses are profitable or close to profitability, and it has about Rs 900 crore in the bank.
“With a topline of around 400 crores, most businesses profitable or near-profitable, and 900 crores in the bank, we had every option to keep going independently. Nobody was forcing this,” he said.
Munjal said discussions with upGrad Chairperson and Co-founder Ronnie Screwvala over the years gradually made the combination more compelling, adding that the absence of financial pressure allowed Unacademy to consider the transaction over time.
In a LinkedIn post, upGrad Chairperson and Co-founder Ronnie Screwvala revealed that conversations around a possible combination first started in 2020, when Munjal met him and upGrad Co-founder Mayank Kumar over lunch in Mumbai.
At that meeting, Munjal had proposed bringing Unacademy and upGrad together and had even suggested that he could run the combined entity. While that proposal did not move ahead at the time, Screwvala said the interaction left an impression.
The conversations resumed more seriously in late July 2025, when Munjal approached Screwvala again and discussed Unacademy’s position and the choices before the company.
“Cut to today. We’re happy to close the Acquisiton and coming together of Unacademy and upGrad,” Screwvala wrote.
For upGrad, Unacademy adds capabilities across consumer learning, product and technology, as well as access to a different audience segment. Screwvala also pointed to the resilience of the Unacademy brand and the team behind it as areas that complement upGrad’s existing business.
“I think there are some incredible strengths that Unacademy brings to what upGrad doesn’t have: the savviness, the product & tech first thinking, the ability to look at a completely different target audience, the brand and the resilience that the team that created this,” Screwvala said.
Both founders also highlighted Airlearn, Unacademy’s language-learning product. Munjal said the app had become one of the three most downloaded language-learning apps globally in less than two years, while Screwvala pointed to it as an example of a consumer technology product built in India gaining traction internationally.
“India to the world is a real opportunity and Airlearn is already showing us a glimpse of it,” Screwvala wrote.
Munjal also reflected on Unacademy’s broader journey, including its free learning platform, educator ecosystem and employee ESOP buybacks, while expressing confidence that shareholders could create further value from the merger.

title: upGrad completes all-stock acquisition of Unacademy Group in $200 million deal
content:
upGrad completes all-stock acquisition of Unacademy Group in $200 million deal
- Published OnSep 1, 2026 | 17:53 IST
- Last Updated OnSep 1, 2026 | 19:23 IST
upGrad has completed its all-stock acquisition of Unacademy Group in a deal valuing the edtech company at just over $200 million, bringing its test-prep and other businesses under the upGrad umbrella.
In a major consolidation within India’s edtech sector, higher education platform upGrad has officially completed its acquisition of Unacademy Group in an all-stock transaction on Tuesday, September 1.
The deal, which was initiated via a term sheet in March 2026 and received clearance from the Competition Commission of India (CCI) in July, values Unacademy Group at just over $200 million. Under the terms of the transaction, Unacademy shareholders receive equity in upGrad.
The acquisition brings Unacademy’s full suite of operating entities, including competitive exam preparation, PrepLadder, creator monetisation platform Graphy, and language-learning app Airlearn, under the upGrad umbrella.
Gaurav Munjal will continue as CEO of Unacademy and will lead the Unacademy Group of businesses within upGrad.
A ₹900 crore cash cushion and profitability push
The deal brings significant cash reserves to upGrad’s consolidated balance sheet. At the time of closing, Unacademy Group reported a topline of approximately ₹400 crore, supported by around ₹900 crore in cash on its balance sheet. The group noted that most of its business lines are currently profitable or approaching profitability.
The combined entity merges upGrad’s higher education, study-abroad, and enterprise upskilling portfolio with Unacademy’s test-prep and consumer-facing verticals. Outside its core test-prep base, Unacademy’s language-learning app Airlearn has scaled to 10 million learners across 150 countries over the last two years, while free educator content across its channels has surpassed 10 billion YouTube views.
"We had ₹900 crore in the bank and every option to keep going alone," said Gaurav Munjal, Co-founder and CEO of Unacademy Group. "We chose this instead because building it with Ronnie, together with upGrad, is the more ambitious path, not the safer one."
Full-stack EdTech consolidation
The move marks one of the largest structural integrations in Asian edtech, spanning K-12 competitive exams through postgraduate education and corporate workforce development.
"With upGrad and Unacademy coming together, we will now reach learners at every stage, from their first competitive exam to the last skill they pick up at work," said Ronnie Screwvala, Co-founder and Chairperson of upGrad.
The company confirmed that all Unacademy Group products, existing subscriptions, course batches, and educator contracts will continue to operate without disruption. Unacademy employees and business teams will transition over to upGrad alongside their respective operating units.

title: upGrad completes $200 million acquisition of Unacademy
content:
Brands
upGrad completes $200 million acquisition of Unacademy
100 per cent share swap gives upGrad access to Unacademy’s test prep business
MUMBAI: The edtech classroom just got a little more crowded and a lot more consolidated. Ronnie Screwvala-led upGrad has completed its acquisition of Unacademy for just over $200 million, bringing two of India’s prominent education platforms under one roof after months of negotiations.
The transaction, valued at Rs 1,955 crore, was structured as a 100 per cent share swap, with Unacademy investors set to receive one seat on upGrad’s board. Ronnie Screwvala announced the completion of the deal in a LinkedIn post.
For upGrad, the acquisition marks a significant expansion beyond its established businesses in higher education, professional learning, study abroad and upskilling. Unacademy brings a sizeable online test-preparation operation covering UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE, along with its language-learning platform Airlearn.
The deal also represents a dramatic reset in Unacademy’s valuation story. The company reached a peak valuation of $3.44 billion in 2021. Its latest transaction value puts the acquisition at more than 90 per cent below that peak.
Yet the numbers around the current business paint a more nuanced picture. Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal said the company currently has a topline of around Rs 400 crore, while most of its businesses are profitable or close to profitability. It also has Rs 900 crore in cash.
The road to the acquisition has been anything but straight.
Discussions began in November last year, but were called off in January amid differences over valuation. The two companies revived negotiations in March, eventually settling on the share-swap structure.
The Competition Commission of India cleared the combination on July 7, paving the way for the transaction to close.
Screwvala said the relationship between the two companies goes back further, recalling an initial conversation in 2020, when Munjal approached him and upGrad co-founder Mayank Kumar about bringing the businesses together.
That proposal did not move forward at the time, but Screwvala said it demonstrated the scale of what Unacademy was building. The conversations resurfaced in July 2025, when Munjal again approached upGrad.
The combination brings together distinctly different positions in India’s education market.
upGrad has built its business around higher education, professional learning, career progression and international education, while Unacademy has a stronger consumer-facing identity in test preparation and online learning.
Munjal will continue to lead Unacademy following the acquisition.
Unacademy’s educator ecosystem has generated more than 10 billion views on YouTube, according to Munjal. Airlearn, meanwhile, became one of the world’s three most-downloaded language-learning apps in less than two years, and will also become part of the combined portfolio.
For upGrad, that adds not only a test-preparation business but also another consumer brand and a technology-led product ecosystem.
The acquisition arrives as India’s edtech sector moves away from the pandemic-era obsession with rapid expansion and sky-high valuations towards profitability, sustainability and consolidation.
With Unacademy now folded into upGrad, the deal effectively joins two different sides of India’s education market, one focused on career advancement and higher education, the other on mass-market learning and competitive examinations.
The next test will be whether the promised synergies can turn that combination into a stronger education business, rather than simply a bigger one.

He said the company had raised funds during a peak period but exited at a much lower valuation, adding that he did not want to hide the reality of the transaction.

Company highlights impact beyond valuation
Munjal pointed to Unacademy’s broader contribution to online education, including the rise of popular educators whose YouTube content collectively crossed 10 billion views.

While Unacademy did not fully capture the financial value of its original mission to democratise education, Munjal said the company changed the structure of online learning in India and influenced the wider industry.

title: UpGrad completes $200 million-plus acquisition of Unacademy
content:
UpGrad has completed its acquisition of Unacademy for just over $200 million, marking the close of a deal that values the edtech company more than 90% below its $3.4-billion peak valuation in 2021, according to a report by the Economic Times.

Unacademy was valued at $3.4 billion in 2021, after which the Indian edtech sector went through a period of cost-cutting, business exits and consolidation as pandemic-era online learning growth slowed and funding conditions tightened.

“Sometimes, you are drawn towards a path that is more exciting than the one that makes you more money,” he added.
The two companies had been in discussions for several months before upGrad signed a term sheet in March for an all-stock transaction, with Munjal expected to continue as CEO, as per a report by Moneycontrol.

title: Unacademy’s $3.44 billion valuation to $200 million acquisition by upGrad: Gaurav Munjal reflects on journey
content:
Edtech company upGrad, led by Ronnie Screwvala, completed its buyout of Unacademy for over $200 million. The deal was confirmed on Tuesday in a post on X by Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal. Munjal, in his social media post, said, "Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200M." However, he added, “We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that.” The sale price was a fraction of the edtech company's peak valuation of $3.44 billion. The company was started by Munjal along with co-founders Roman Saini, Hemesh Singh, and Sumit Jain. Munjal said that when the company was started, their first goal was to 'democratise education'. Munjal said that while the company was not able to completely capture the economic value of the mission, it did manage to change the face of online education in India, and several of its products ended up becoming the template that the sector would go on to follow. "When @RomanSaini and I started Unacademy with @hemezh and @sumjain, the mission was to democratise education. We didn't end up capturing all the economic value of that mission. But we changed what online education looks like in this country, and the products we built became the template for the entire sector," he said. In his post, Munjal also highlighted the importance of educators and how his free platform helped create an entire generation of celebrity educators. He pointed out that the total YouTube videos by Unacademy's educators have touched 100 billion views. "Unacademy's free platform created a generation of celebrity educators. Educators are a cornerstone of any economy, and they should be celebrated, and our platform enabled that in our country," Munjal said. He also spoke of Airlearn, which, as per his post, became one of the top 3 most downloaded language-learning apps in the entire world within two years of its launch. "We always wanted to build a global consumer product out of India. We did," he said. Munjal said that the company had a topline of around ₹400 crore, while it had ₹900 crore in the bank, which gave them enough cushion required to go on independently. "Nobody was forcing this. But sometimes, you are drawn towards a path that is more exciting than the one that makes you more money," he said regarding the decision to sell the company. Munjal also admired Ronnie Screwvala in his post, saying that he was inspired by the latter's vision for education in India. "I always walked away with the thought that it would be fantastic to work with him," he said, adding that since there was no pressure of running out of money, there was time to think the decision through. "The more we did, the clearer it got: this is a better path for the ecosystem, not just for us," he added. In his post, Munjal also thanked other startup founders without whom he said he would have "personally given up when things got really hard: Shailendra Singh, Deepinder Goyal, Bhavin Turakhia, Sujeet Kumar, Bhavish Aggarwal, Aakrit Vaish, Mukul Arora, Shantanu Rastogi and Karthik Reddy." content:
Unacademy acquired by upGrad for just over $200 million; Munjal says ‘we raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction’

Unacademy has completed its acquisition by Ronnie Screwvala-led upGrad for just over $200 million, marking the end of a months-long transaction between two of India’s major edtech companies. Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal confirmed the closure in a post on X on Tuesday.
“Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200M. We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I’m not going to dress these facts up,” Munjal said.
The Competition Commission of India (CCI) had cleared the transaction on July 7, according to its notification. The regulator approved the acquisition of certain shareholding in Sorting Hat Technologies Pvt Ltd, the legal entity that operates Unacademy, and its subsequent merger with and into upGrad Education Pvt Ltd. The CCI said the detailed order would follow.
The transaction is a 100% share-swap deal. Earlier reports put its value at around ₹1,955 crore to ₹2,055 crore, or roughly $218 million. The deal represents a sharp fall from Unacademy’s peak valuation of about $3.44 billion in 2021.
Why Unacademy chose upGrad
Munjal said the decision to sell was not driven by a shortage of cash. He said Unacademy currently has a topline of around ₹400 crore, with most of its businesses profitable or near-profitable, and ₹900 crore in the bank.
“With a topline of around 400 crores, most businesses profitable or near-profitable, and 900 crores in the bank, we had every option to keep going independently. Nobody was forcing this,” he said.
Munjal said his interactions with Screwvala and his understanding of what upGrad had built in higher education eventually convinced him that a combination would be better for the wider education ecosystem.
“Sometimes, you are drawn towards a path that is more exciting than the one that makes you more money,” he said.
The deal also gives upGrad an entry into online test preparation, including categories such as UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE, where it previously did not have a presence. The transaction had been structured as an acquisition of shareholding in Sorting Hat Technologies followed by its merger with upGrad Education.
From unicorn to acquisition
Looking back at Unacademy’s journey, Munjal said the company did not capture all the economic value of its original mission to democratise education, but changed the way online education was built in India.
“When Roman Saini and I started Unacademy with Hemez and Sumit Jain, the mission was to democratise education,” he said. “We didn’t end up capturing all the economic value of that mission. But we changed what online education looks like in this country.”
He highlighted Unacademy’s free platform, which helped create a generation of celebrity educators. Their YouTube videos, he said, have crossed 10 billion views.
Munjal also pointed to Airlearn, the language-learning business launched by Unacademy, saying it became one of the top three most-downloaded language-learning apps globally in less than two years.
“We always wanted to build a global consumer product out of India. We did,” he said. Munjal also thanked employees, educators, investors and his co-founders, while highlighting Unacademy’s four ESOP buybacks.
“We did four ESOP buybacks that created real value for our employees, even though the founders and investors didn’t create much for themselves in the process,” he said.
Munjal is expected to continue as CEO of Unacademy following the transaction, while Unacademy shareholders will receive shares in upGrad as part of the all-stock combination.

Munjal said Unacademy had also completed four ESOP buybacks, which he described as creating value for employees even as founders and investors did not create comparable value for themselves.
He said he now looked forward to the next phase under the upGrad umbrella and was confident that shareholders would create significant value from the merger.

title: India’s Unacademy sells to rival upGrad for $206M, about 94% less than its peak valuation
content:
Unacademy, once one of India’s most valuable edtech startups, has been acquired by rival upGrad at a valuation of just over $200 million, about 94% less than its 2021 peak valuation.
The all-stock deal values Unacademy at ₹19.55 billion (about $206 million), upGrad’s co-founder and chairperson Ronnie Screwvala told TechCrunch. Unacademy shareholders are receiving upGrad shares as part of the transaction, while angel investors were cashed out at closing, Screwvala said.
On Monday, Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal said in a post on X that the deal had closed, nearly six months after the transaction was first announced in March. The Bengaluru-based startup, backed by SoftBank, Tiger Global, General Atlantic, and other global investors, was valued at $3.44 billion at its peak in 2021.
“We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that,” he wrote. “I’m not going to dress these facts up.”
The deal comes despite Unacademy having about ₹9 billion (about $94.8 million) in the bank and annual revenue of roughly ₹4 billion (around $42.13 million), Munjal wrote. He said most of the startup’s businesses were profitable or close to profitability, and said the company had the option to continue operating independently.
Founded in 2015, Unacademy spent heavily in 2020 and 2021 as it battled rivals such as Byju’s for students and educators as pandemic lockdowns sent demand for online learning soaring. However, after physical classes reopened and demand for edtech plummeted, the startup cut costs, laid off employees, and restructured parts of its business.
Unacademy eventually brought most of its businesses to profitability or close to it, Munjal said. “Nobody was forcing this,” he wrote.
Nonetheless, Unacademy’s leadership had come to believe that getting the startup to the scale or an eventual public listing would require expanding into more areas of education, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Joining upGrad, which has built a larger presence in offline education, offered one route to doing that, the sources told TechCrunch.
Airlearn, Unacademy’s language-learning app, is also part of the transaction, and will remain under upGrad for now. Screwvala said upGrad was “very excited and positive” about the business.
However, in about six months, Munjal and Screwvala are expected to decide whether to continue building the about 25-person business internally or raise external capital for it, according to one of the people.
Late last year, Munjal had explored raising external capital for Airlearn and received term sheets from investors, but ultimately abandoned those plans as talks with upGrad progressed, the person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch.
“To see a product coming out of India gaining traction globally is a great example of what is possible when the thinking, product and ambition are not limited by geography. India to the world is a very real opportunity, and Airlearn is already showing us a glimpse of it,” Screwvala wrote on X.
The two-year-old online platform serves 10 million users across over 150 countries, Unacademy said. The edtech group overall has amassed over 10 billion views for its free education videos on YouTube.
The Unacademy brand will be retained, and the deal covers the entire group, including PrepLadder and Graphy. Munjal will continue as Unacademy’s CEO and lead the business as before, with a focus on its online operations and Airlearn, Screwvala told TechCrunch.
No layoffs are planned, according to one of the people familiar with the matter. Unacademy Group has about 1,000 employees.
Unacademy raised about $880 million across 13 funding rounds, per Tracxn. The sale follows a sharp reversal for India’s edtech industry after the rapid growth it saw during the pandemic. Byju’s, once valued at $22 billion and India’s most valuable startup, saw its valuation effectively fall to zero and entered insolvency proceedings in 2024.

title: Unacademy closes UpGrad deal at $200 Mn
content:
Edtech major Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over $200 million, marking a 94% decline from its peak valuation of around $3.4 billion in 2021.
Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal confirmed the completion of the deal in a post on Tuesday, acknowledging that the company had raised money at its peak but was now being sold at a fraction of that valuation.
Entrackr had exclusively reported earlier that UpGrad was set to close the acquisition of Unacademy in a deal valued at around Rs 1,955 crore. The transaction was structured as an all-stock deal, with Munjal expected to continue leading Unacademy following the combination.
Interestingly, Munjal said the deal was not driven by a cash crunch. According to him, Unacademy currently has a topline of around Rs 400 crore, with most of its businesses either profitable or near profitable. The company also has around Rs 900 crore in the bank, he added.
According to Munjal, Unacademy had the option to continue independently but chose to combine with UpGrad after discussions with Screwvala and a belief that the merger would create a stronger education ecosystem.
The acquisition gives UpGrad an entry into the online test-preparation segment, including categories such as UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE. It also adds Unacademy’s educator network and other businesses to UpGrad’s existing higher education, upskilling and study-abroad portfolio.
Munjal also highlighted Unacademy’s broader impact, saying its educators have crossed 10 billion views on YouTube. He added that the company conducted four ESOP buybacks that created liquidity for employees.
While the exit value is far below Unacademy’s peak valuation, Munjal said he remains confident that shareholders can create significant value from the combined business going forward.

title: From $3.5 Bn To $200 Mn: upGrad Completes Unacademy Acquisition
content: After months of negotiations and regulatory clearances, edtech major upGrad has completed its acquisition of Unacademy in a deal valued at just over $200 Mn. Unacademy cofounder Gaurav Munjal announced the closure of the transaction in a post on X today. “We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I’m not going to dress these facts up. The talks did not progress at the time but were revived in late July 2025, when Munjal reached out again as Unacademy found itself at a “crossroads”. He said Unacademy would bring product- and tech-focused thinking, a strong consumer brand, and access to a different target audience to upGrad. Screwvala also highlighted the global potential of Unacademy’s language-learning platform Airlearn, saying its traction demonstrated the opportunity to build consumer education products in India for global markets. “I think there are some incredible strengths that Unacademy brings to what upGrad doesn’t have: the savviness, the product and tech-first thinking, the ability to look at a completely different target audience, the brand and the resilience that the team that created this,” Screwvala said. At the time of the acquisition, Unacademy had a topline of around ₹400 Cr and about ₹900 Cr in the bank, while most of its businesses were profitable or close to profitability, he claimed. “With a topline of around 400 Cr, most businesses profitable or near-profitable, and 900 Cr in the bank, we had every option to keep going independently. Nobody was forcing this,” Munjal said. Explaining the rationale behind the deal, he said working with Screwvala and joining upGrad offered a more compelling path for Unacademy than continuing independently. Munjal added that he expects Unacademy’s shareholders to create “immense value” from the merger. He also thanked the startup’s employees and said its two previous ESOP buybacks created value for them, even though its founders and investors did not generate significant returns in the transaction. How Unacademy Went From $3.5 Bn To $200 Mn Founded in 2015 by Munjal, Roman Saini, and Hemesh Singh, Unacademy began as a YouTube channel before expanding into an online learning platform focused on competitive examination preparation. However, the reopening of offline educational institutions hit demand for online learning, prompting Unacademy to undertake multiple rounds of layoffs, reduce its cash burn, and shut or scale down several verticals. title: Unacademy Now Part of UpGrad, Acquisition Deal Completed for Over $200 Million
content:
The transaction is more than 90% below Unacademy’s peak valuation of $3.44 billion in 2021.
UpGrad, led by Ronnie Screwvala, has completed the acquisition of Unacademy. Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal confirmed the completion of the deal through a social media post on September 1, 2026. The two companies had been in discussions over the acquisition for several months.
The transaction has been completed entirely through a share-swap arrangement. According to reports, the final transaction value has been set at around INR 1,955 crore, which translates to slightly more than $200 million. Existing Unacademy investors will receive shares in UpGrad. Gaurav Munjal will continue as the CEO of Unacademy following the acquisition.
Deal Completed at More Than 90% Below $3.44 Billion Peak Valuation
Unacademy had reached a valuation of around $3.44 billion in 2021, when the company was among India’s leading edtech unicorns. However, following the pandemic, the funding and valuation environment in the edtech sector changed significantly. Companies began focusing more on profitability and sustainable business models rather than rapid expansion.
After the completion of the deal, Gaurav Munjal said that the company was acquired at a much lower valuation compared with the peak valuation at which it had raised funding. He acknowledged the gap openly and said that Unacademy had played an important role in changing the way online education was delivered in India.
Acquisition Not Driven by Cash Shortage
According to Gaurav Munjal, Unacademy did not take the decision because of financial pressure or a shortage of cash. He said the company has a topline of around INR 400 crore, while most of its businesses are profitable or close to profitability. The company also has around INR 900 crore in cash.
This meant that Unacademy had the option to continue operating independently. However, after discussions with UpGrad founder Ronnie Screwvala and considering the potential combination of the two businesses, the company decided to move forward with the deal. Munjal said the decision was not driven only by financial considerations but also by the larger opportunity the combination could create for the education ecosystem.
UpGrad Gets Strong Entry into Online Test Preparation
The acquisition will give UpGrad a stronger presence in the online test preparation segment. Unacademy is known for preparing students for competitive examinations such as UPSC, JEE, NEET and GATE.
Unacademy’s test preparation business will now be combined with UpGrad’s existing higher education, professional upskilling, certification and study-abroad businesses. In information submitted to the Competition Commission of India (CCI), UpGrad had also stated that the combination would give it entry into the online test preparation segment, where it previously had limited presence.
CCI Approval Received in July
The regulatory process for the deal has also been completed. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) approved the acquisition of certain shareholding in Sorting Hat Technologies and its subsequent merger with UpGrad Education on July 7, 2026. Sorting Hat Technologies operates Unacademy.
The discussions between the two companies progressed through several stages. According to reports, talks around the acquisition began in November 2025 and faced delays due to differences over valuation. The companies later signed a term sheet for the all-stock transaction in March 2026.
Unacademy Built a Strong Identity in Online Education
Unacademy was founded by Gaurav Munjal, Roman Saini, Hemesh Singh and Sumit Jain. The company played an important role in popularising online education for competitive examination preparation on a large scale in India.
According to Munjal, videos by Unacademy educators have collectively crossed more than 10 billion views on YouTube. The company also launched Airlearn in the language-learning segment, which, according to Munjal, became one of the three most-downloaded language-learning apps globally in less than two years.
During its journey, the company also completed four ESOP buybacks for employees. Munjal said these transactions created value for employees, although the financial outcome for founders and investors was not as strong as the company’s peak valuation had suggested.
A New Phase for India’s Edtech Sector
The combination of UpGrad and Unacademy reflects the growing consolidation in India’s edtech market. While Unacademy has a strong presence in competitive examinations and test preparation, UpGrad is known for its presence in higher education, professional skilling and career-focused learning.
The combination will give UpGrad an opportunity to reach new student segments and bring different areas of education under a larger platform. For Unacademy, the acquisition marks a new phase in its journey from an independent startup to becoming part of a larger education group.

title: Left IAS, built Unacademy: How Roman Saini co-founded edtech firm now acquired by upGrad for $200 million
content:
Unacademy’s acquisition by Ronnie Screwvala-led upGrad has brought the edtech company's growth journey back into focus, while also turning attention to the entrepreneurs who built it.
Among them is Roman Saini, who took an unusual route into entrepreneurship. An AIIMS graduate who cleared the UPSC Civil Services Examination and joined the Indian Administrative Service, Saini left the bureaucracy to build an education technology company with Gaurav Munjal, Hemesh Singh and Sumit Jain.
On September 1, 2026, Unacademy co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal announced that upGrad had completed the acquisition of the company for just over $200 million (Rs 1,897 crore). The transaction represents a reset from Unacademy’s peak valuation of $3.44 billion (Rs 32,628 crore) in 2021.
The deal marks a very different point in Unacademy’s journey from the pandemic-era edtech boom, when the company rapidly expanded its operations and attracted hundreds of millions of dollars from global investors.
Roman Saini's career before Unacademy was already unusual. He cleared the medical entrance examination at 16 and went on to study medicine at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. He completed his MBBS and subsequently worked as a junior resident at AIIMS.
At 22, Saini cleared the UPSC Civil Services Examination in his first attempt, securing All India Rank 18. He joined the 2014 batch of the IAS and was allotted the Madhya Pradesh cadre.
His stint in government, however, was short. After roughly a year and six months in the civil services, Saini resigned and moved into entrepreneurship. His decision came as he was already involved in helping UPSC aspirants through online education.
That experience eventually became the foundation for his next career move.
The co-founder of Unacademy, Gaurav Munjal, had started uploading educational videos on YouTube in 2010. The initiative eventually evolved into a formal business in 2015 when Munjal joined hands with Roman Saini and Hemesh Singh.
Munjal, an engineering graduate, had a technology and product background. Singh had experience in building web and mobile products, while Saini brought experience as a doctor, civil servant and educator focused on competitive examinations.
The business model was built around using technology to distribute educational content at scale. Instead of relying exclusively on physical coaching centres, Unacademy brought educators and students onto an online platform, initially focusing heavily on competitive examinations.
Over time, the company expanded beyond UPSC preparation into areas including IIT-JEE, NEET and other examinations.
The business scaled rapidly as online education gained traction.
By 2021, Unacademy had become one of India's most prominent edtech companies, with more than 50,000 registered educators and lakhs of learners. The company also expanded its presence across thousands of Indian cities and multiple languages.
The growth attracted some of the biggest names in global venture capital.
In August 2021, Unacademy raised $440 million in a Series H funding round led by Temasek, with participation from General Atlantic, Tiger Global, SoftBank Vision Fund 2 and Mirae Asset. The round valued the company at $3.44 billion.
That valuation was almost 10 times the company's valuation about 18 months earlier. By then, Unacademy had raised roughly $860 million in total funding.
The company also expanded through acquisitions, including PrepLadder, Kreatryx, Coursavy and CodeChef, as it attempted to build a broader education and career platform.
For Roman Saini, the journey had moved from medicine to government service and then into one of India’s largest venture-backed startups.
However, the growth trajectory changed as the pandemic-driven online education boom faded.
The acquisition price of just over $200 million is a fraction of Unacademy's $3.44 billion peak valuation. Munjal himself acknowledged the gap, saying the company had raised capital at its peak but was being sold at a fraction of that valuation.
Reflecting on the acquisition, Saini said the decision to leave the IAS was made during a phone call with Munjal while he was at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), the civil services training academy in Mussoorie.
“Unacademy is getting acquired by upGrad today. It has been one helluva journey since that stroll in LBSNAA when I was on the phone with Gaurav Munjal and decided to quit IAS and build Unacademy,” Saini said in a post on X.
Saini also recalled the scale Unacademy reached during the Covid-19 pandemic. At its peak, he said, the platform hosted more than 100,000 live classes a month and had nearly 1 million paid subscribers.
Unacademy is getting acquired by upGrad today. It has been one helluva journey since that stroll in LBSNAA when I was on the phone with @gauravmunjal and decided to quit IAS and build Unacademy.
At one point during peak Covid, there were more than 100,000 live classes happening… — Roman Saini (@RomanSaini) September 1, 2026
He said the platform's early focus was on bringing educators online at a time when relatively few established teachers were teaching digitally. Saini recalled calling around 200 people within the first month to persuade them to teach online.
“There are only very few top educators in India today who haven't at some point taught on Unacademy,” Saini said, highlighting the platform's role in the expansion of India's online education ecosystem.
Saini also recalled some of the challenges of building the company, including working through nights when growth slowed and travelling to China with Munjal to meet an investor who ultimately did not turn up.
Looking ahead, Saini said Unacademy’s integration with upGrad would give the business an opportunity to expand further. “As a part of upGrad, we are looking forward to creating an even bigger dent in the universe with Ronnie Screwvala,” he said.
For Roman Saini, the Unacademy story represents a rare entrepreneurial transition: from being trained to work as a doctor and then serving as an IAS officer, to becoming one of the early builders of India's digital education industry.
